# AGENTS.md

## Имя проекта
Имя текущего проекта 
`UartDebug2`

## Язык и кодировка

1. Отвечать пользователю на русском языке, если он пишет по-русски.
2. Все Markdown-файлы (`*.md`) в этой папке должны читаться и записываться как UTF-8.
3. Если кириллический текст выглядит поврежденным, сначала проверь, что файл читается как UTF-8.

## Общие правила работы

### Стиль работы
1. Задавай вопросы в непонятной ситуации. 
2. Не бойся возражать пользователю. 
3. Предлагай свои варианты выполнения очередного шага или этапа. 
4. Предложения и советы делай короткими и по существу вопроса. 

### Переход к очередному шагу работы
1. Спроси, что будем делать на очередном шаге. 
2. Выслушай предложения пользователя. 
3. Приведи свои возражения и предложения. 
4. Веди диалог до тех пор, когда пользователь предложит выполнить этот шаг. 
5. Перед изменениями кратко объяснять, что будет сделано. 
6. Любое создание, изменение или удаление файла выполняй только после явного разрешения пользователя. 
7. После корректировки файла или файлов сообщи коротко, что ты сделал. 

## Особенность ввода пользователя

У пользователя бывают ошибки ввода с клавиатуры.
Признаки ошибочного ввода:
1. Текст выглядит оборванным. 
2. Текст заканчивается случайными буквами или символами. 
3. Текст не имеет смысла. 
В случае ошибочного ввода не выполняй это действие. Спроси пользователя о необходимости продолжения этого действия. 

## Правила анализа

При проверке файлов обращай внимание на:

1. внутренние противоречия;
2. неполные правила;
3. дублирующие определения;
4. расхождение терминов;
5. ошибки в нумерации;
6. неработающие ссылки внутри Markdown;
7. грамматические ошибки и описки;
8. несоответствие между логикой, отображением и действиями пользователя.

Если найдено противоречие, укажи:

1. где оно находится;
2. в чем именно проблема;
3. почему это может повлиять на будущую реализацию;
4. возможный вариант исправления.

## Версии проекта

При работе над проектом ведется система версий. 
Версия проекта состоит из двух цифр, например: 
Version 2.1
В этом примере 2 - это версия, 1 - это подверсия. 
В пректе могут быть файлы с версиями, например: 
Version 2.1.3 
В этом примере файл относится к версии проекта 2.1 . При этом версия самого файла в пределах проекта - 3. 
Версия проекта должна совпадать со старшими значениями версии проекта.
Файлы с одниаковыми версиями полностью совместимы в пределах одного проекта. Файлы с разными версиями внутри одного проекта могут оказаться несовместимыми. В таком случае нужно обратить внимание пользователя на это обстоятельтво. 
Команда "Привести версию файла к версии проекта" означает увеличить версию файла (наименование версии) к такому состоянию, что две старших цифры версии файла станут равными версии проекта. 
Приведение версии файла в проекте можно делать только в сторону увеличения значений. 
В версии файла может быть буква, например:
Version 2.1.3-d
Такая запись означает редакцию файла. Разные редакции файла в пределах одной версии файла полностью совместимы. С точки зрения функциональности такие файлы идентичны. 
При переходе к следующей версии файла сначала редакция будет отсутствовать. Буквы редакции появляются только после правки начальной версии файла. 
В случаен существования разных версий и редкций файлов в проекте актуальным (применяемым к обработке) нужно считать файл с самой старшей вресией или редакцией. 

## Имена файлов
Полное имя файла определяется так, как это принято в операционных системах - имя файла и расширение. 
Расширение указывает на функциональное назначение файла. 
Например, файлы с расширением md - этот текстовые файлы с разметкой маркдаун. 
Имя файла в наших проектах может состоять из нескольких частей. Например: 
Project_descrition_01 Ver.2.1.3-a (en).md
Тут: 
Project_descrition_01 - это содержательное имя файла. Из этого имени можно понять, что этот файл является описанием проекта 01. 
Далее через пробел может идти версия файла. В нашем случае это версия (редакция) Ver.2.1.3-a 
Часть имени с версией необязательна. На файл со значением версии в имени файла могут быть ссылки как на файл Project_descrition_01.md
Далее через пробел в скобках может идти информация о языке или о цели этого файла. Эта часть имени необязательна. Она может быть опущена. Ссылка на файл без указания имени эквивалентна ссылке на файл с полным именм. 
В скобках могут быть признаки языков, например
en - английский язык
ru - русский язык
es - испанский язык
de - немецкий
fr - французский
ai - текст специально предназначен для Искусственного Интеллекта. 
### Пример ссылки на файлы. 
Например, где-то в описаниях будет укзано, что файлы 
Project_structures.md 
должны быть обработаны каким-то образом. Это означает, что это относится к любому из файлов, как это привдено ниже
Project_structures.md 
Project_structures Ver.2.5.2.md 
Project_structures Ver.2.5.4.md 
Project_structures Ver.2.5.2-b.md 
Project_structures Ver.2.5.2-b (ru).md - русский вариант файла
Project_structures (en).md

### Цифры в начале имени файла
Если в начале имен файлов есть цифры, например 01_ , то это означает, что такие файлы нужно рассматривать по порядку этих цифр. 

### Цифра в скобках в конце имени файла
Если в конце имени файла имеется цифра в скобках, например, 
Какой_то_файл(2).md
То это ничего не означает. Это значит, что в текущей папке оказались два файла с одинаковым именем. В этом случае нужно оперировать с файлм с наибольшей цифрой в таких скобках. 

## Добавление правил в процессе работы
По мере работы над проектом возможна корректировка этих правил. 
Все изменения ты должен вносить в файл 
Project_Rules/AGENTS_Add_On.md
Каждое дополнение к правилам основного файла нужно помещать в этот файл. 
Каждое дополнение должно иметь очередной порядковый номер. 
Новые записи в файл Project_Rules/AGENTS_Add_On.md ты должен вносить по явной команде польователя. 

## Папки проекта
Все папки проекта доступны для чтения, создания и удаления файлов, для редактирования файлов. 
Папка 
`Notes/`
предназначена для текущих и рабочих заметок по мере развития проекта. Файл, находящиеся в этой папке не предназначены для ИИ.

## 1. Применение периферии и других аппаратных ресурсов

### 1.1. Условия компиляции

- Подключи необходимые заголовочные файлы с помощью `#include`.

- Не дублируй вручную определения регистров, битовых масок и других символов, уже предоставленных заголовочным файлом выбранного микроконтроллера.
- Проверь, что значения проектных макросов соответствуют фактической конфигурации программы и аппаратуры.

### 1.5. Инициализация ресурса

Если запись конфигурации требует ожидания готовности регистра перед записью и/или ожидания завершения синхронизации после записи, циклы ожидания и запись регистра оформляй как единую группу без пустых строк. Разные регистры или самостоятельные этапы инициализации разделяй пустой строкой.

Пустой цикл ожидания записывай в одну строку с фигурными скобками. Например:

```c
while ((PERIPHERAL.STATUS & REGISTER_BUSY_bm) != 0u) {}
PERIPHERAL.REGISTER = required_value;
while ((PERIPHERAL.STATUS & REGISTER_BUSY_bm) != 0u) {}
```

Это правило определяет оформление, но не требует автоматически добавлять оба ожидания. Необходимость проверки до записи, после записи или с обеих сторон и используемый флаг устанавливаются правилами конкретного периферийного устройства.

## 2. Использование значений регистров после сброса

При первичной инициализации после сброса не выполняй отдельную запись только ради значения, которое регистр уже имеет после сброса, если это значение проверено по даташиту. Когда состояние могло измениться или настройка выполняется повторно, задавай нужное значение явно.

## 3. Безопасное включение выходов

# Нерешённые проблемы технических материалов

Этот файл предназначен для регистрации противоречий и неясностей, обнаруженных в исходных документах и пока не разрешённых по другим авторитетным источникам.

## PRB-USART-001 - Противоречие в значении STATUS после сброса

**Состояние:** не решено.

### Описание проблемы

В описании регистра `USARTn.STATUS` приведены два несовместимых значения после сброса:

- в заголовке регистра указано `Reset: 0x00`;
- в строке сброса отдельных битов для `DREIF` указано значение `1`, а для остальных определённых битов - `0`.

Если `DREIF` действительно равен единице, полное значение регистра после сброса должно соответствовать `0x20`, а не `0x00`.

Проблема влияет на код, который сразу после сброса проверяет готовность передатчика или полагается на первоначальное состояние `DREIF`.

### Исходный источник

- Документ: [ATtiny1624/1626/1627 Data Sheet, DS40002234B](tinyAVR_2_series/ATtiny1624_1626_1627/ATtiny1624-26-27-DataSheet-DS40002234B.pdf).
- Глава 24, `USART - Universal Synchronous and Asynchronous Receiver and Transmitter`.
- Печатная страница и страница PDF: 311.
- Раздел 24.5.5, `USART Status Register`.
- Противоречащие места: поле `Reset: 0x00` в заголовке регистра и значение `1` для `DREIF` в строке `Reset` битовой таблицы.

### Места в производных материалах

- [ATtiny162x_USART_Universal_Synchronous_Asynchronous_Receiver_Transmitter.md](tinyAVR_2_series/ATtiny1624_1626_1627/USART/ATtiny162x_USART_Universal_Synchronous_Asynchronous_Receiver_Transmitter.md), раздел `12.1. STATUS reset-value discrepancy in the source`.
- [ATtiny162x_USART_Model.yaml](tinyAVR_2_series/ATtiny1624_1626_1627/USART/ATtiny162x_USART_Model.yaml):
  - `registers.STATUS.reset_header`;
  - `registers.STATUS.reset_from_bit_row`;
  - первая запись в `source_discrepancies`.

### Что требуется для решения

Проверить значение после сброса по актуальному errata, другому официальному документу Microchip или экспериментально на микроконтроллере. До проверки код не должен полагаться на одно из двух значений без явной проверки `DREIF`.

## PRB-USART-002 - Противоречие в допустимости CLK2X для асинхронного режима

**Состояние:** не решено.

### Описание проблемы

Описание поля `USARTn.CTRLB.RXMODE` утверждает, что при `CMODE = ASYNCHRONOUS` или `CMODE = IRCOM` в `RXMODE` всегда следует записывать `NORMAL` (`0x00`). Это противоречит другим частям той же главы, где `CLK2X` (`0x01`) явно описан как Double-Speed режим асинхронной работы с восемью выборками на бит.

Вероятно, в описании `RXMODE` допущена ошибка в названии режима, однако глава 24 сама по себе не позволяет доказать правильную формулировку.

Проблема влияет на выбор режима при расчёте скорости передачи, значения `BAUD` и допустимой ошибки частоты.

### Исходный источник

- Документ: [ATtiny1624/1626/1627 Data Sheet, DS40002234B](tinyAVR_2_series/ATtiny1624_1626_1627/ATtiny1624-26-27-DataSheet-DS40002234B.pdf).
- Глава 24, `USART - Universal Synchronous and Asynchronous Receiver and Transmitter`.
- Противоречащее ограничение: печатная страница и страница PDF 314, раздел 24.5.7, `Control B`, описание `RXMODE = NORMAL`.
- Противоположное утверждение: печатная страница и страница PDF 300, раздел 24.3.3.2.4, `Double-Speed Operation`.
- Связанные подтверждающие места: формулы и описания асинхронной выборки на страницах 293 и 298-300.

### Места в производных материалах

- [ATtiny162x_USART_Universal_Synchronous_Asynchronous_Receiver_Transmitter.md](tinyAVR_2_series/ATtiny1624_1626_1627/USART/ATtiny162x_USART_Universal_Synchronous_Asynchronous_Receiver_Transmitter.md):
  - раздел `8.3. Asynchronous operation`;
  - раздел `12.2. RXMODE restriction discrepancy in the source`.
- [ATtiny162x_USART_Model.yaml](tinyAVR_2_series/ATtiny1624_1626_1627/USART/ATtiny162x_USART_Model.yaml):
  - `communication_modes.asynchronous.rx_modes`;
  - вторая запись в `source_discrepancies`.

### Что требуется для решения

Проверить правильное ограничение `RXMODE` по актуальному errata или другому официальному документу Microchip. До проверки применение `CLK2X` должно сопровождаться ссылкой на это противоречие.

## PRB-TCB-001 - Несогласованные имена байтов CCMP в режиме PWM8

**Состояние:** не решено.

### Описание проблемы

В строке `8-Bit PWM mode` таблицы условий установки флага `CAPT` используются обозначения `CCML` и `CCMH`. Однако описание регистра `TCBn.CCMP` и остальные части главы определяют два независимых байта режима PWM8 как `CCMPL` и `CCMPH`.

Вероятнее всего, в таблице пропущена буква `P`, но сама глава не содержит явного исправления. Проблема влияет на точное сопоставление формулировки таблицы с именами регистров и символами заголовочного файла.

### Исходный источник

- Документ: [ATtiny1624/1626/1627 Data Sheet, DS40002234B](tinyAVR_2_series/ATtiny1624_1626_1627/ATtiny1624-26-27-DataSheet-DS40002234B.pdf).
- Глава 22, `TCB - 16-Bit Timer/Counter Type B`.
- Печатная страница и страница PDF: 260.
- Раздел 22.5.5, `Interrupt Flags`, таблица 22-6, строка `8-Bit PWM mode`: `CCMH` и `CCML`.
- Связанное место: страница 265, раздел 22.5.10, `Capture/Compare`: `CCMPH` и `CCMPL`.

### Места в производных материалах

- [ATtiny162x_TCB_16_Bit_Timer_Counter_Type_B.md](tinyAVR_2_series/ATtiny1624_1626_1627/TCB/ATtiny162x_TCB_16_Bit_Timer_Counter_Type_B.md), раздел `6.8. 8-bit PWM mode`.
- [ATtiny162x_TCB_Model.yaml](tinyAVR_2_series/ATtiny1624_1626_1627/TCB/ATtiny162x_TCB_Model.yaml):
  - `modes.PWM8`;
  - первая запись в `source_discrepancies`.

### Что требуется для решения

Проверить обозначения по актуальному errata или более новой официальной редакции документа. До проверки в производных материалах следует использовать документированные имена регистров `CCMPL` и `CCMPH`, одновременно сохраняя ссылку на ошибочную строку таблицы 22-6.

# ATtiny1624/1626/1627 GPIO: Practical Use Cases and Verified Guidance

## 1. Purpose and evidence

This is a practical companion to [ATtiny162x_PORT_IO_Pin_Configuration.md](ATtiny162x_PORT_IO_Pin_Configuration.md), not a replacement for its register reference. The use cases are inspired by Microchip's *Getting Started with General Purpose Input/Output (GPIO)* (TB3229, DS90003229B, 2021). TB3229 explicitly covers tinyAVR 0- and 1-series, megaAVR 0-series, and AVR DA devices; its bare-metal code targets ATmega4809, **not** ATtiny1624/1626/1627. Device-specific claims and names below were therefore checked against the ATtiny1624/1626/1627 data sheet, revision DS40002234B, and the supplied device headers. [S1, Introduction; S2, §§3.1, 17]

The C fragments illustrate individual tasks; they are not a complete, compiled application. The current workspace does not provide `avr-gcc` for a build check. Choose the electrical circuit, clock, timing source, and any other enabled peripherals before integrating them.

### Source key

- **S1:** [Getting-Started-with-GPIO-DS90003229B.pdf](Getting-Started-with-GPIO-DS90003229B.pdf), especially printed pp. 7-14; [Microchip's companion ATmega4809 examples](https://github.com/microchip-pic-avr-examples/atmega4809-getting-started-with-gpio-mplab).
- **S2:** [ATtiny1624-26-27-DataSheet-DS40002234B.pdf](../ATtiny1624-26-27-DataSheet-DS40002234B.pdf), especially printed p. 18 (pin multiplexing) and pp. 147-170 (PORT); [the same revision on Microchip's site](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/ATtiny1624-26-27-DataSheet-DS40002234B.pdf).
- **S3:** Supplied [ATtiny1624](../iotn1624.h), [ATtiny1626](../iotn1626.h), and [ATtiny1627](../iotn1627.h) device headers. They confirm the PORT register members, `PIN6_bm`, `PIN7_bm`, `PORT_PULLUPEN_bm`, `PORT_ISC_*_gc`, `PORTA_PORT_vect`, and `SLPCTRL_SMODE_PDOWN_gc` used or discussed here. Their presence does not by itself prove that an example builds with a particular compiler installation.
- **S4:** avr-libc documentation for [interrupts](https://www.nongnu.org/avr-libc/user-manual/group__avr__interrupts.html), [atomic blocks](https://www.nongnu.org/avr-libc/user-manual/group__util__atomic.html), [sleep](https://www.nongnu.org/avr-libc/user-manual/group__avr__sleep.html), and [delays](https://www.nongnu.org/avr-libc/user-manual/group__util__delay.html). These document the C-level ISR, global-interrupt, atomic-access, race-safe sleep, and delay APIs; the device data sheet remains authoritative for wake-up capability.

## 2. A pin pair available on all three devices

The examples use **PA6 for a button** and **PA7 for an LED**. Both are bonded out in the packages listed below. PA6 is one of the `Px6` pins with fully asynchronous interrupt detection, which is useful for wake-up while `CLK_PER` is stopped. PA0 is deliberately avoided because it also carries RESET/UPDI. These pin choices are illustrative: a board using PA6/PA7 for another peripheral needs a different allocation. [S2, p. 18, table 3-1 and note 2]

| Device/package | PA6 package pin | PA7 package pin |
|---|---:|---:|
| ATtiny1624, SOIC/TSSOP-14 | 4 | 5 |
| ATtiny1626, SOIC/SSOP-20 | 4 | 5 |
| ATtiny1626, VQFN-20 | 7 | 8 |
| ATtiny1627, VQFN-24 | 7 | 8 |

Assumed circuit: the button connects PA6 to GND when pressed; the internal pull-up establishes a high level when released. The LED connects from PA7 to GND through an appropriate current-limiting resistor, so a high output turns it on. Verify resistor value and allowable pin current against the electrical specifications and the actual LED; neither is determined by the GPIO register description. [S1, pp. 9-10; S2, p. 18]

## 3. Initialize and operate a simple GPIO pair

```c
#include <avr/io.h>
#include <stdint.h>

#define BUTTON_bm PIN6_bm  /* PA6 */
#define LED_bm    PIN7_bm  /* PA7 */

void gpio_init(void)
{
    PORTA.OUTCLR = LED_bm;  /* Prepare the LED's initial OFF level. */
    PORTA.DIRSET = LED_bm;  /* Enable the PA7 output driver. */

    PORTA.DIRCLR = BUTTON_bm; /* PA6 is input-only. */
    PORTA.PIN6CTRL = PORT_PULLUPEN_bm | PORT_ISC_INTDISABLE_gc;
    /* PA6: pull-up on, input buffer on, pin interrupt off, inversion off. */
}

uint8_t button_is_pressed(void)
{
    return (PORTA.IN & BUTTON_bm) == 0u; /* Active-low button. */
}

void led_on(void)  { PORTA.OUTSET = LED_bm; }
void led_off(void) { PORTA.OUTCLR = LED_bm; }
void led_toggle(void) { PORTA.OUTTGL = LED_bm; }
```

`DIRSET`, `DIRCLR`, `OUTSET`, `OUTCLR`, and `OUTTGL` act only on bits written as `1`; no read-modify-write is needed for these selected-bit changes. Preparing `OUT` before enabling `DIR` avoids briefly driving an unwanted initial value. The latter ordering is an engineering recommendation inferred from the registers, not a separate hardware guarantee. `PIN6CTRL` is an ordinary per-pin control register: the full assignment above intentionally clears any previous inversion and sense configuration. In an existing application, preserve fields that must remain set. [S2, pp. 149, 155-161, 165]

For a continuously blinking LED, call `led_toggle()` from a correctly configured periodic timer or, for a simple blocking demonstration, between delays. A delay duration is meaningful only when the application's clock frequency and delay implementation are known. Do not copy ATmega4809 board pin assignments or clock assumptions from TB3229. [S1, pp. 8-9]

For lowest power, an output that never needs to be read as an input may have its digital input buffer disabled through its own `PINnCTRL.ISC`. Do **not** disable PA6's input buffer while reading `PORTA.IN` or using its pin interrupt. Apply the same check to unused pins, analog inputs, UPDI, and peripheral-controlled pins before changing them. [S1, p. 7; S2, pp. 149-150, 165]

## 4. Short versus long button press

TB3229's polling example measures the time between press and release with a counter and delay. The transferable idea is the **state sequence**, not its hard-coded timing or ATmega4809 pin numbers: [S1, pp. 10-11]

1. Start from a confirmed released state (`PA6 = 1`).
2. Accept a press only after the input has remained low for an application-chosen debounce interval.
3. Record the press time using a timer or other known time base.
4. Accept release only after the input has remained high for the debounce interval.
5. Compare the elapsed press time with the application's short/long threshold and act once per accepted press-release cycle.

The 10 ms delay used for contact bounce elsewhere in TB3229 is an **example policy**, not a guaranteed debounce duration for every switch. Select the interval from the actual switch and responsiveness requirements. A blocking delay can miss other work; a timer-driven state machine is preferable when the application has concurrent tasks. These are software-design recommendations, not PORT hardware specifications. [S1, pp. 10-13]

## 5. Button interrupt: what is device-specific

For PA6, select both-edge sensing if the application needs a notification on both press and release. A PORT interrupt vector can be shared by the pins of that PORT. If more than one pin interrupt can be enabled, inspect `INTFLAGS` to identify every pending source. If PA6 is guaranteed to be the only enabled source for the complete program, its handler may directly clear and service the known PA6 flag without first testing it. The example below keeps the source check so that other PORTA pin interrupts can be added without changing its dispatch structure. Clear a pin's flag by writing `1` **directly** to that flag bit. Do not use a read-modify-write operation such as `PORTA.INTFLAGS |= BUTTON_bm`, which could also clear other already-pending write-one-to-clear flags. [S2, pp. 150, 163, 165; S3]

```c
#include <avr/interrupt.h>

static volatile uint8_t button_edge_pending;

void button_interrupt_enable(void)
{
    PORTA.DIRCLR = BUTTON_bm;
    PORTA.PIN6CTRL = PORT_PULLUPEN_bm | PORT_ISC_INTDISABLE_gc;
    PORTA.INTFLAGS = BUTTON_bm; /* Clear a stale PA6 flag (write one). */
    PORTA.PIN6CTRL = PORT_PULLUPEN_bm | PORT_ISC_BOTHEDGES_gc;
    sei(); /* Enable global interrupts after the relevant setup is complete. */
}

ISR(PORTA_PORT_vect)
{
    uint8_t flags = PORTA.INTFLAGS;
    if ((flags & BUTTON_bm) != 0u) {
        PORTA.INTFLAGS = BUTTON_bm; /* Clear only PA6's flag. */
        button_edge_pending = 1u;   /* Defer interpretation/debounce. */
    }
    /* Handle any other enabled PORTA pin flags here as well. */
}
```

`button_edge_pending` coalesces events; it does **not** count every transition. If the main loop consumes and clears it while interrupts can update it, make that exchange atomic (for example with avr-libc's `ATOMIC_BLOCK(ATOMIC_RESTORESTATE)` from `<util/atomic.h>`). After an edge, determine the stable pressed/released state in main-line code; mechanical bounce can generate several interrupts. Keeping the ISR short and deferring the debounce decision follows TB3229's application pattern. [S1, pp. 12-13; S4]

## 6. Wake-up on button press and release

The hardware capability is not identical for every pin. The ATtiny162x data sheet identifies `Px2` and `Px6` as fully asynchronous. Fully asynchronous pins can wake the device from sleep modes with `CLK_PER` stopped for any enabled interrupt sense configuration. For partially asynchronous pins in that situation, only `BOTHEDGES` or `LEVEL` are listed, and the required pin level must persist until the clock restarts; otherwise wake-up may occur without an interrupt. Therefore PA6 plus `BOTHEDGES` is a suitable **hardware starting point** for press/release wake-up, but the actual circuit and firmware still need testing. [S2, p. 18; pp. 151-152]

Application sequence: configure PA6 and its interrupt, select the desired sleep mode, enable global interrupts, enter sleep, then process the flagged edge after wake-up. Do not turn the LED on or off based solely on which edge was requested: after a debounce interval, sample the current PA6 level and use the confirmed button state. If a switch bounces, the final stable level matters more than an individual interrupt. [S1, pp. 12-13; S2, pp. 151, 165]

The simple `sleep_mode()` macro can have a race when the application tests for pending work immediately before sleeping. avr-libc documents a test-and-sleep pattern using `cli()`, `sleep_enable()`, `sei()`, `sleep_cpu()`, and `sleep_disable()`. Use that pattern when integrating a pending-event test; do not assume that `if (!pending) sleep_mode();` is race-free. Confirm the selected sleep mode, wake sources, and toolchain macros for the final build. [S4, sleep documentation]

## 7. Limits of transfer from TB3229

| TB3229 item | Treatment for ATtiny1624/1626/1627 |
|---|---|
| LED blink and active-low button examples | Transfer the method; select pins using the ATtiny162x pin table and board schematic. |
| `PORTx.DIR/OUT/IN`, pull-up, and `ISC` | Confirmed for these devices by their data sheet and all three headers. |
| Interrupt and Power-Down example | Recheck the ATtiny162x asynchronous-sensing class, wake-up conditions, other enabled PORT flags, and test-and-sleep race. |
| Code exactly as printed | Not a drop-in program. In particular, TB3229 p. 13 uses `PORTB.INTFLAGS &= PIN2_bm`; direct mask assignment is clearer for ATtiny162x write-one-to-clear flags. TB3229 pp. 9 and 11 also disagree on the delay header; the avr-libc header is `<util/delay.h>`. |
| MCC pin configuration | Relevant only if the project uses MCC; generated names and configuration must be checked against the selected ATtiny162x device and tool version. |

No example in this file has been claimed as compiled or hardware-tested. Before deployment, build for the exact MCU and compiler package, check its pinout and peripheral allocation, then test LED polarity, pull-up behavior, bounce, interrupt flag handling, and wake-up on the target board.

# ATtiny1624/1626/1627 GPIO Source Guide

This file routes GPIO work to the smallest relevant set of sources. It applies to ATtiny1624, ATtiny1626, and ATtiny1627; confirm the exact device, package, board connections, and task before choosing pins or writing code. Follow the project instructions regardless of the reading order below.

## Reading order

1. Start here when the task concerns GPIO on one of these devices. Then read the [general AVR programming rules](../../../AVR_Programming_General_Rules.md) and [GPIO working rules](ATtiny162x_Working_Rules_GPIO.md). These describe the preferred approach, not the hardware specification.
2. Open only the task-relevant reference: the [pin-multiplexing table](../ATtiny162x_Pin_Multiplexing.yaml) for package pins, alternate functions, and pin availability; the [PORT configuration reference](ATtiny162x_PORT_IO_Pin_Configuration.md) for GPIO behavior and registers; the [practical use cases](ATtiny162x_GPIO_Practical_Use_Cases.md) for application patterns. Read more than one when the task crosses those boundaries.
3. When writing C, verify register members, bit masks, enum values, and vector names in the header for the **selected device**: [ATtiny1624](../iotn1624.h), [ATtiny1626](../iotn1626.h), or [ATtiny1627](../iotn1627.h). The supplied headers are reference copies; confirm against the installed toolchain when building.
4. For internal PORT signal relationships, consult the [block model](ATtiny162x_PORT_Block_Model.yaml); use the [diagram](ATtiny162x_PORT_Block_Diagram.svg) when a visual trace is needed. Neither replaces the data sheet.
5. If a needed device-specific fact is absent, unclear, or contradictory, inspect the relevant pages of the [ATtiny1624/1626/1627 data sheet](../ATtiny1624-26-27-DataSheet-DS40002234B.pdf). Start with p. 18 for pins and chapter 17 for PORT, then consult other sections as the question requires. Do not read the entire PDF by default.
6. Consult [TB3229](Getting-Started-with-GPIO-DS90003229B.pdf) only for additional GPIO techniques or examples not sufficiently covered above. Its bare-metal examples target ATmega4809; transfer a technique to ATtiny162x only after checking this device's data sheet and header.

## When to use the Internet

Search when the user asks for online verification; local sources leave an important fact unresolved or conflict; current compiler, library, toolchain, errata, or revision information is needed; or the answer depends on electrical or system details outside the local references. Prefer current primary sources, especially Microchip documentation for hardware facts and official toolchain documentation for software behavior. Distinguish verified facts from inference. If the user restricts the task to local sources, state any unresolved gap instead of silently using external information.

## Do not read by default

- [Additional_GPIO_Files](Additional_GPIO_Files/) is an archive. Open it only on explicit request or for a specific version/history comparison; do not treat its copies as active guidance.
- Do not open all device headers, the entire data sheet, or unrelated peripheral material for a narrow GPIO question.
- Do not treat TB3229 examples, the block model, or project working preferences as overriding the device data sheet.

Reading order is not authority order. For ATtiny162x hardware facts, the applicable device data sheet is authoritative; verify C symbol names against the selected device header. If a local summary, example, or working rule appears to disagree, report the discrepancy rather than silently choosing one.

# ATtiny1624/1626/1627 PORT - I/O Pin Configuration

## 1. Purpose and source

This document is a working reference for configuring and using the PORT peripheral on ATtiny1624, ATtiny1626, and ATtiny1627. It condenses the register descriptions and operating rules needed for GPIO code without reproducing the repeated register-page layout of the data sheet.

- Primary source: `../ATtiny1624-26-27-DataSheet-DS40002234B.pdf`, revision DS40002234B (2021), chapter 17, "PORT - I/O Pin Configuration."
- Pages reviewed: 147 and 149-170. Page 148, the PORT block diagram, was handled separately in `ATtiny162x_PORT_Block_Diagram.svg` and `ATtiny162x_PORT_Block_Model.yaml`.
- Scope: PORT and VPORT behavior described in chapter 17. Package pin numbers, peripheral routes, electrical limits, and the detailed behavior of connected peripherals require other sources.

This is a derived engineering reference, not a substitute for the data sheet. Statements labeled **Practice** are implementation recommendations inferred from the documented register behavior; they are not additional hardware specifications.

## 2. Naming and basic model

Each PORT instance controls a group of up to eight pins. Instances are named `PORTA`, `PORTB`, `PORTC`, and so on. `Pxn` means pin `n` of port `x`: for example, `PA3` corresponds to bit 3 of the PORTA registers. Which symbolic pins are present on a particular device and package must be checked separately.

For each pin, the basic GPIO state is represented by:

| Bit | Function |
|---|---|
| `PORTx.DIR[n]` | Enables or disables the output driver. It does not control the digital input buffer. |
| `PORTx.OUT[n]` | Stores the value used by the output driver when enabled. |
| `PORTx.IN[n]` | Reports the synchronized digital input value while the digital input buffer is enabled. |

`DIR[n] = 0` disables the output driver (input-only configuration); `DIR[n] = 1` enables it (output configuration). With the output driver enabled, `OUT[n] = 0` drives low and `OUT[n] = 1` drives high, subject to pin inversion or peripheral override. The input path is separately configurable, so the pin can normally be read through `IN[n]` even when it is configured as an output.

`PORTx.IN` is synchronized to the peripheral clock, `CLK_PER`. It is a sampled input, not a copy of the `OUT` register. If the digital input buffer is disabled, the corresponding `IN[n]` bit is not updated and must not be treated as a fresh measurement.

After reset, output drivers are tri-stated and digital input buffers are enabled, even when no clock is running. The chapter 17 register reset values shown below are `0x00`. A pin reserved for a special function, such as a debugger connection, may require different handling.

## 3. Basic initialization and GPIO operations

The following operations are optional and depend on the intended pin use:

1. Set or clear direction by writing a `1` to the pin bit of `PORTx.DIRSET` or `PORTx.DIRCLR`.
2. Set or clear the stored output value through `PORTx.OUTSET` or `PORTx.OUTCLR`.
3. Read the pin through `PORTx.IN` if its digital input buffer is enabled.
4. Configure inversion, pull-up, and input sensing in the individual `PORTx.PINnCTRL` register.

**Practice:** For an output with a required initial level, write `OUTSET` or `OUTCLR` before enabling its driver through `DIRSET`. This avoids briefly driving the previous `OUT` value.

Illustrative C code for `PA1`, assuming a device header exposes the register names:

```c
PORTA.OUTCLR = (1u << 1); /* Prepare a low output value. */
PORTA.DIRSET = (1u << 1); /* Then enable the PA1 output driver. */
```

For an input, clear the direction bit and use an `ISC` setting that leaves the digital input buffer enabled:

```c
PORTA.DIRCLR = (1u << 2);
PORTA.PIN2CTRL = 0x00u; /* ISC=INTDISABLE; inversion and pull-up off. */

if ((PORTA.IN & (1u << 2)) != 0u) {
    /* The sampled logical input is high. */
}
```

These examples use numeric bit masks derived from the bit positions in chapter 17. Project code may use named masks from the installed device header instead; their exact spelling is not defined by this chapter.

## 4. Hardware set, clear, and toggle operations

The dedicated `SET`, `CLR`, and `TGL` registers change selected bits without a software read-modify-write of the full `DIR` or `OUT` register:

| Write target | Effect of writing `1` to bit `n` | Effect of writing `0` |
|---|---|---|
| `DIRSET` | Set `DIR[n]`; enable output driver | No effect |
| `DIRCLR` | Clear `DIR[n]`; disable output driver | No effect |
| `DIRTGL` | Toggle `DIR[n]` | No effect |
| `OUTSET` | Set `OUT[n]` | No effect |
| `OUTCLR` | Clear `OUT[n]` | No effect |
| `OUTTGL` | Toggle `OUT[n]` | No effect |

Reading any of the three direction aliases returns the current `DIR` value. Reading any of the three output aliases returns the current `OUT` value.

Writes to independent masks do not alter unrelated pins. For example:

```c
PORTA.OUTSET = (1u << 1);
PORTA.OUTCLR = (1u << 2);
PORTA.OUTTGL = (1u << 3);
```

The second and third statements do not change `OUT[1]`, because their bit-1 write value is zero. Multiple pins may be changed in one operation by OR-ing their masks.

**Practice:** Use these hardware aliases for selected bits. Write `DIR` or `OUT` directly only when replacing the complete port value is intended. A whole-byte software read-modify-write can also disturb bits changed by another execution context between its read and write.

### 4.1 Writing to `IN` is a toggle operation

Both `PORTx.IN` and its VPORT mapping can be written. This does **not** set an input value:

- Writing `0` to bit `n` has no effect.
- Writing `1` to bit `n` toggles the corresponding `PORTx.OUT[n]` bit.

```c
PORTA.IN = (1u << 1); /* Toggles OUT[1]; does not configure an input. */
```

**Practice:** Treat `IN` primarily as a read register; write it only when the output-toggle effect is intentional.

## 5. Individual pin control: `PORTx.PINnCTRL`

`PINnCTRL` is located at offset `0x10 + n` from the PORTx base address, for `n = 0..7`. Each register resets to `0x00`.

| Bit(s) | Field | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | `INVEN` | Invert the pin's input and output operation. |
| 6:4 | Reserved | Do not assign a meaning or write a nonzero value. |
| 3 | `PULLUPEN` | Enable the internal pull-up while the pin is input-only. |
| 2:0 | `ISC` | Select input-buffer and interrupt-sense behavior. |

### 5.1 Inverted I/O: `INVEN`

`INVEN = 0` leaves input and output values non-inverted; `INVEN = 1` inverts them. The functional description explicitly names inverted behavior for `IN`, `OUT`, `OUTSET`, and `OUTTGL` operations. The block diagram shows inversion on both the output and digital input paths.

Changing `INVEN` causes an edge on the pin. Enabled interrupt/event logic and other peripherals using the pin can observe that edge. Do not silently change inversion while such consumers are active.

### 5.2 Pull-up: `PULLUPEN`

`PULLUPEN = 1` requests the internal pull-up while the pin is configured as input-only. The pull-up is disconnected when the pin is configured as an output, even if this bit remains set. `PULLUPEN = 0` disables the pull-up.

### 5.3 Input/sense configuration: `ISC[2:0]`

| Value | Setting | Digital input buffer | Interrupt condition |
|---:|---|---|---|
| `0x0` | `INTDISABLE` | Enabled | Interrupt disabled |
| `0x1` | `BOTHEDGES` | Enabled | Both edges |
| `0x2` | `RISING` | Enabled | Rising edge |
| `0x3` | `FALLING` | Enabled | Falling edge |
| `0x4` | `INPUT_DISABLE` | Disabled | Interrupt disabled |
| `0x5` | `LEVEL` | Enabled | Low level |
| `0x6`, `0x7` | Reserved | - | Do not use |

`INPUT_DISABLE` stops updating the corresponding `IN` bit. Disabling the digital input buffer on unused pins and pins used for analog input/output is recommended by the data sheet for lowest power consumption; it may also reduce analog-input noise.

The chapter provides a low-level sense mode, not a separate high-level sense mode. When writing only one field of an already configured `PINnCTRL`, preserve the other fields and reserved bits. Unlike `DIR` and `OUT`, `PINnCTRL` has no dedicated set/clear/toggle aliases in this chapter.

## 6. Port-wide slew-rate control

`PORTx.PORTCTRL` contains `SRL` at bit 0:

| `SRL` | Effect |
|---:|---|
| `0` | Slew-rate limitation disabled for all pins of PORTx. |
| `1` | Slew-rate limitation enabled for all pins of PORTx. |

This is a port-wide control, not an individual-pin option. Electrical values and timing are outside chapter 17 and must be checked in the Electrical Characteristics section.

## 7. PORT interrupts and flags

Each pin can be selected as an interrupt source through its `PINnCTRL.ISC` field. When the selected pin condition occurs, `PORTx.INTFLAGS.INT[n]` is set. An interrupt request is generated when the source is enabled and the flag is set; the request remains active until the flag is cleared. The chapter lists a PORTx interrupt vector for the port, with per-pin causes in `INTFLAGS`.

`INTFLAGS` uses write-one-to-clear semantics:

- Writing `0` to bit `n` has no effect.
- Writing `1` to bit `n` clears that pin's flag.

```c
unsigned char pending = PORTA.INTFLAGS;
PORTA.INTFLAGS = pending; /* Clear the flags observed in the snapshot. */
```

**Practice:** Clear a known flag with a direct mask assignment, for example `PORTA.INTFLAGS = (1u << 2);`. Avoid `PORTA.INTFLAGS |= mask`: its read-modify-write sequence can write `1` to other already-set W1C flags and clear them too. The same flag semantics apply through `VPORTx.INTFLAGS`.

Take care when changing sense settings:

1. If `INVEN` changes in the same cycle as `ISC`, the inversion-induced edge may not generate an interrupt request.
2. If an input is disabled while an interrupt is being synchronized, a request may appear when input sensing is re-enabled, even with a different interrupt setting.
3. If `ISC` is changed while an interrupt is being synchronized, that interrupt may not be requested.

The chapter does not specify the C interrupt-handler symbol or global CPU interrupt setup. Obtain those from the selected device header and CPU documentation.

## 8. Asynchronous sensing and wake-up

All PORT pins support asynchronous input sensing, but the capabilities of fully and partially asynchronous pins differ. Chapter 17 refers to the I/O Multiplexing and Considerations section to identify which pins are fully asynchronous; do not infer a pin's class from its PORT letter or pin number alone.

| Property | Partially asynchronous pin | Fully asynchronous pin |
|---|---|---|
| Wake-up with `CLK_PER` running | Any enabled interrupt sense configuration | Any enabled interrupt sense configuration |
| Wake-up with `CLK_PER` stopped | Only `BOTHEDGES` or `LEVEL` | Any enabled interrupt sense configuration |
| Minimum pulse width with `CLK_PER` running | At least one `CLK_PER` cycle | Less than one `CLK_PER` cycle |
| Requirement with `CLK_PER` stopped | Pin value must remain until `CLK_PER` restarts | Less than one `CLK_PER` cycle |
| Interrupt dead-time after the previous interrupt | No new interrupt for three `CLK_PER` cycles | Less than one `CLK_PER` cycle |

The source table merges the fully asynchronous "less than one `CLK_PER` cycle" cell across its last three rows. For a partially asynchronous pin used to wake the MCU while `CLK_PER` is stopped, the required level must persist long enough for wake-up to complete. If it disappears too early, the MCU may wake without generating an interrupt.

## 9. Events

Each physical PORT pin is an asynchronous Event System generator named `PORTx.PINn`. It produces a **level** event representing the pin value; the event lasts as long as the corresponding level. There are as many PORT event generators as there are PORT pins on the device.

The event output is the value on the pin while its digital input buffer is enabled. If that buffer is disabled, the corresponding Event System output is zero. PORT has no event inputs. Event routing and consumer configuration belong to EVSYS, outside chapter 17.

## 10. Sleep and debug behavior

- Apart from interrupts and input synchronization, pin configurations are independent of sleep mode.
- PORT always uses `CLK_PER`; input synchronization halts when that clock stops.
- Pins can wake the device subject to the asynchronous-sensing restrictions in section 8 above.
- A peripheral connected to a PORT pin may have its own sleep-mode behavior, which must be checked in its documentation.
- When the CPU is halted in Debug mode, PORT continues normal operation. Functions requiring periodic CPU servicing, such as interrupt-driven processing, may malfunction or lose data while the CPU is halted.

## 11. Peripheral override

USARTs, ADCs, timers, and other peripherals can connect to pins. A peripheral may have a primary and one or more alternate pin routes selected through PORTMUX or a multiplexer inside that peripheral.

Enabling a peripheral can override normal GPIO behavior in a peripheral-dependent way. Some PORT properties may remain under PORT control. The separate block-diagram model shows possible overrides of output direction, output value, and digital-input disable; it does not define the exact conditions for any given peripheral. Unoverridden pins continue to act as GPIO.

Before assigning a pin to a peripheral, determine its availability in the chosen package, any required routing, and the peripheral's specific override rules. Chapter 17 alone is insufficient for this decision.

## 12. PORTx register reference

The offsets below are relative to the PORTx base address. All listed registers reset to `0x00`; not every bit necessarily corresponds to a bonded-out pin on every package.

| Offset | Register | Read result | Write effect |
|---:|---|---|---|
| `0x00` | `DIR` | Current direction | Replace direction byte |
| `0x01` | `DIRSET` | Current `DIR` | Set selected `DIR` bits on written `1`s |
| `0x02` | `DIRCLR` | Current `DIR` | Clear selected `DIR` bits on written `1`s |
| `0x03` | `DIRTGL` | Current `DIR` | Toggle selected `DIR` bits on written `1`s |
| `0x04` | `OUT` | Current output value | Replace output-value byte |
| `0x05` | `OUTSET` | Current `OUT` | Set selected `OUT` bits on written `1`s |
| `0x06` | `OUTCLR` | Current `OUT` | Clear selected `OUT` bits on written `1`s |
| `0x07` | `OUTTGL` | Current `OUT` | Toggle selected `OUT` bits on written `1`s |
| `0x08` | `IN` | Synchronized input value | Toggle selected `OUT` bits on written `1`s |
| `0x09` | `INTFLAGS` | Current per-pin flags | Clear selected flags on written `1`s |
| `0x0A` | `PORTCTRL` | Port-wide control | Bit 0 is `SRL` |
| `0x0B-0x0F` | Reserved | - | Do not write |
| `0x10-0x17` | `PIN0CTRL` ... `PIN7CTRL` | Individual pin control | Configure `INVEN`, `PULLUPEN`, and `ISC` |

For the `SET`, `CLR`, and `TGL` aliases, writing zero to a bit has no effect. `IN` and `INTFLAGS` have their own special write-one semantics and must not be treated as ordinary byte-storage registers.

## 13. VPORTx mapping and use

VPORTx maps four frequently used PORTx registers into I/O register space. Reading or writing a mapped VPORT register has the same hardware outcome as using the corresponding regular PORT register. The I/O register location permits memory-specific bit manipulation instructions with single-cycle bit access; whether a C expression compiles to such an instruction depends on the compiler and expression.

| VPORTx offset | VPORTx register | Mapped regular register |
|---:|---|---|
| `0x00` | `DIR` | `PORTx.DIR` |
| `0x01` | `OUT` | `PORTx.OUT` |
| `0x02` | `IN` | `PORTx.IN` |
| `0x03` | `INTFLAGS` | `PORTx.INTFLAGS` |

All four VPORTx registers reset to `0x00`. VPORTx does **not** provide `DIRSET/CLR/TGL`, `OUTSET/CLR/TGL`, `PORTCTRL`, or `PINnCTRL`.

**Practice:** Use regular PORT aliases for mask-based set/clear/toggle and full pin configuration. Use VPORT when its I/O-space access is beneficial and the generated machine instruction is appropriate. A C whole-byte read-modify-write on `VPORTx.DIR` or `VPORTx.OUT` is not automatically equivalent to a hardware `DIRSET` or `OUTSET` operation.

## 14. Practical code patterns

The examples assume that the project includes a suitable device header defining the PORT register objects. Chapter 17 defines register behavior but not toolchain-specific macro names, interrupt-handler declarations, or build flags.

### 14.1 Input with pull-up and no interrupt

```c
PORTA.DIRCLR = (1u << 2);
PORTA.PIN2CTRL = (1u << 3) | 0x00u; /* PULLUPEN=1, ISC=INTDISABLE. */
```

### 14.2 Falling-edge interrupt sense with pull-up

```c
PORTA.DIRCLR = (1u << 2);
PORTA.PIN2CTRL = (1u << 3) | 0x03u; /* PULLUPEN=1, ISC=FALLING. */
PORTA.INTFLAGS = (1u << 2);        /* Clear a pending PA2 flag. */
```

Global CPU interrupt enable and a correctly named PORTA ISR are separate requirements.

### 14.3 Disable digital input on an unused GPIO pin

```c
PORTA.DIRCLR = (1u << 4);
PORTA.PIN4CTRL = 0x04u; /* ISC=INPUT_DISABLE; pull-up and inversion off. */
```

Apply this only after checking that the pin is truly unused and is not needed by a special function or peripheral. On an analog pin, check that the connected analog peripheral has no conflicting requirement.

### 14.4 Change only `ISC` while retaining other pin settings

```c
PORTA.PIN2CTRL = (PORTA.PIN2CTRL & (unsigned char)~0x07u) | 0x03u;
```

This is a software read-modify-write of one pin's control register. It preserves `INVEN` and `PULLUPEN`, but it is not the hardware mask operation provided for `DIR` and `OUT`; consider concurrent access before using it.

## 15. Checklist for later code generation

1. Select the exact MCU and package, then map the physical package pin to `Pxn` using pin-multiplexing data.
2. Check whether a peripheral or special function owns the pin and whether PORTMUX routing is required.
3. Set the desired `OUT` value before enabling a GPIO output driver.
4. Prefer `DIRSET/CLR/TGL` and `OUTSET/CLR/TGL` for selected bits.
5. Keep the digital input buffer enabled if the program must read `IN`, sense an interrupt, or emit the pin's event level.
6. Use `INPUT_DISABLE` for truly unused or suitable analog-function pins when minimizing power/noise.
7. Clear `INTFLAGS` by writing `1` to only the intended flags.
8. Confirm the pin's fully/partially asynchronous class before relying on wake-up with `CLK_PER` stopped.
9. Do not confuse a stored `OUT` value with the synchronized value read from `IN`.
10. Do not write `IN` unless toggling `OUT` is intentional.
11. Do not use reserved `ISC` values or write reserved control bits.
12. Remember that `SRL` applies to the whole PORT instance.

## 16. Information not supplied by chapter 17

Other data-sheet sections or the selected device header are needed for:

- physical package pin numbers and availability of individual `Pxn` signals;
- which pins are fully rather than partially asynchronous;
- peripheral pin alternatives, exact PORTMUX values, and peripheral-specific override behavior;
- electrical limits, pull-up characteristics, and slew-rate timing;
- C macro spellings, interrupt vector names, and compiler-specific code generation;
- global interrupt setup and detailed EVSYS routing.

# ATtiny1624/1626/1627 Working Rules: GPIO

These are **project working rules**, not a Microchip publication or a replacement for the device data sheet. They record preferred engineering decisions for GPIO on ATtiny1624, ATtiny1626, and ATtiny1627. Apply a rule only when its stated conditions hold; check the board schematic and the exact MCU/package before writing code. Hardware facts come from the ATtiny162x data sheet and device headers. Application preferences are identified as such.

This file intentionally does not repeat the register reference in [ATtiny162x_PORT_IO_Pin_Configuration.md](ATtiny162x_PORT_IO_Pin_Configuration.md), the pin table in [ATtiny162x_Pin_Multiplexing.yaml](../ATtiny162x_Pin_Multiplexing.yaml), or the examples in [ATtiny162x_GPIO_Practical_Use_Cases.md](ATtiny162x_GPIO_Practical_Use_Cases.md).

## WR-GPIO-01: Confirm ownership before configuring a pin

Before configuring GPIO, check that the pin exists on the selected device and package, how it is connected on the board, and how it is assigned in software, including UPDI/RESET, peripherals, and `PORTMUX`. A pin name in a device header does not mean that the pin is free. [D, p. 18 and §17.3.2.5; M]

## WR-GPIO-02: Define the safe state before enabling an output

Before `DIRSET`, use `OUTSET` or `OUTCLR` to establish a level safe for the circuit, accounting for load polarity and `INVEN`: on repeated initialization, `OUT` may contain a different value. If a safe state is required already during reset, provide it with an external pull resistor or driver; firmware does not yet control the pin. [D, §§17.3.1-17.3.2, 17.5; P]

## WR-GPIO-03: Give truly unconnected pins a defined physical level

**Project preference:** For a truly unconnected pin (see WR-GPIO-01), leave `DIR=0`, enable `PULLUPEN`, and set `ISC=INPUT_DISABLE`: after initialization, the pin has a defined high level and the digital input is disabled. The internal pull-up is inactive during reset; if the level matters then too, use an external pull resistor. Do not enable the internal pull-up when using an external pull-down. [D, §§17.3.1, 17.3.2.3, 17.5.12; L; K]

## WR-GPIO-04: Keep digital input sensing enabled when it is needed

For a digital input, clear its `DIR` bit and choose a `PINnCTRL.ISC` setting that leaves the digital input buffer enabled. For an active-low button connected to GND, an internal pull-up can establish the released-high state. If a full `PINnCTRL` assignment is appropriate, `PORT_PULLUPEN_bm` alone also sets `ISC = INTDISABLE`, because that field's value is zero. `INPUT_DISABLE` is different: it stops fresh updates of `PORTx.IN` and disables the pin interrupt. Do not use it for a pin that must be read, generate an interrupt, or supply its digital level to EVSYS. [D, §§17.3.2.3, 17.3.4, 17.5.12; H]

**Integration exception:** A full assignment to `PINnCTRL` also changes `INVEN` and other fields. Preserve required existing settings when a pin is shared with other code.

For a pin used only as a digital output, selecting `INPUT_DISABLE` may be used as an optional power-saving measure, but it is not required for output operation and does not establish the initial output level. Do not add it automatically to a minimal output example. Apply it only after confirming that software does not read the pin through `PORTx.IN`, the pin does not generate an interrupt or supply its digital level to EVSYS, and no assigned peripheral function requires its input buffer. Establish a safe initial output level through `OUTSET` or `OUTCLR` as specified by WR-GPIO-02.

## WR-GPIO-05: Separate analog pin preparation from ADC setup

For a pin selected as an analog input, disable its output driver and internal pull-up, and normally select `INPUT_DISABLE` for the digital input buffer. This may reduce power consumption and analog noise. Verify the pin-to-analog-signal mapping first. `PORTx.IN` is not a valid fresh digital sample while the buffer is disabled. Configuring the ADC or analog comparator is a separate task and is **not** accomplished by the PORT settings alone. [D, p. 18 and §§17.3.1, 17.3.2.3, 17.5.12; M]

## WR-GPIO-06: Use mask-write aliases for ordinary bit changes

Use `DIRSET/DIRCLR` and `OUTSET/OUTCLR/OUTTGL` when changing selected bits without disturbing unrelated output or direction bits. Write a `1` only in each target bit; zero bits have no effect. Prefer explicit `OUTSET`/`OUTCLR` over `OUTTGL` when the required resulting state must be known, especially for safety-relevant loads. A C read-modify-write of the whole `DIR` or `OUT` register is not the same operation as a hardware set/clear alias when another execution context may change other bits. [D, §§17.3.2.1, 17.5.1-17.5.8]

## WR-GPIO-07: For minimum cycle count, verify VPORT instructions

`VPORTx` maps `DIR`, `OUT`, `IN`, and `INTFLAGS` into I/O space. On these AVRxt devices, `SBI` and `CBI` each take one CPU clock and can change one bit of a suitable VPORT register. For example, an optimized build may turn `VPORTA.OUT |= PIN3_bm` and `VPORTA.OUT &= ~PIN3_bm` into `SBI` and `CBI` for PA3. **Do not claim a C statement takes one cycle without inspecting the generated assembly.** Regular `PORTx.OUTSET/OUTCLR` remains the straightforward choice unless the measured timing requirement calls for VPORT. [D, §17.3.2.4; H; I]

Writing `1` to a `PORTx.IN` or corresponding `VPORTx.IN` bit toggles `OUT[n]`; this is a special write operation, not a way to set an input value. Use it only when the toggle is intentional and its generated instruction has been checked. [D, §§17.3.2.1, 17.5.9, 17.7]

## WR-GPIO-08: Treat PORT interrupt flags as write-one-to-clear

A PORT vector can cover multiple pins. When more than one pin interrupt is enabled for a PORT, inspect `PORTx.INTFLAGS` to identify every pending source and clear only the flags that are actually serviced by directly writing their masks, for example `PORTA.INTFLAGS = PIN6_bm;`.

When exactly one pin interrupt is enabled for a PORT and this remains a guaranteed invariant of the complete program, the ISR may directly clear and service that known flag without first reading `INTFLAGS`. Do not use this simplification if another pin can also be enabled as an interrupt source for the same PORT vector. Avoid `|=` on `INTFLAGS`: its read-modify-write can clear other flags already set to `1`. Keep an ISR short; transfer button interpretation and debouncing to application code. If main-line code and an ISR exchange state, account for atomic access. [D, §§17.3.3, 17.5.10; P; A]

## WR-GPIO-09: Validate wake-up against the chosen pin and sleep mode

Do not treat all PORT pins as equally asynchronous. The device pin table identifies `Px2` and `Px6` as fully asynchronous. With `CLK_PER` stopped, partially asynchronous pins support wake-up only for the listed `BOTHEDGES` or `LEVEL` configurations and need the required level held through wake-up; otherwise the MCU may wake without a pin interrupt. Check the selected pin, `ISC`, sleep mode, pulse duration, and application test-and-sleep sequence. [D, p. 18 and §§17.3.3.1, 17.3.5; A]

## WR-GPIO-10: Verify each implementation at its actual boundary

Before calling code production-ready, confirm the exact package and schematic, device-header names, pin polarity, initial/reset state, other peripheral ownership, and any electrical limits outside the PORT chapter. Compile for the exact MCU and inspect assembly when instruction timing matters. Test the circuit, particularly loads that must stay inactive during reset and inputs that can bounce. Examples in this folder are not automatically compiled or hardware-tested. [D; H; M; P]
