# ATtiny1624/1626/1627 Working Rules: RTC and PIT

These are **project working rules** for using the Real-Time Counter (RTC) and Periodic Interrupt Timer (PIT) on ATtiny1624, ATtiny1626, and ATtiny1627 with the MPLAB XC8 compiler for AVR. Hardware behavior must be verified against the device data sheet, and compiler-specific behavior must be verified against the MPLAB XC8 documentation and the headers supplied with the selected device pack.

## WR-RTC-01: Establish scope and compilation context

Apply these rules together with the [general AVR programming rules](../../../AVR_Programming_General_Rules.md). Use [ATtiny162x_RTC_Real_Time_Counter.md](ATtiny162x_RTC_Real_Time_Counter.md) and [ATtiny162x_RTC_Model.yaml](ATtiny162x_RTC_Model.yaml) for device-specific hardware facts. Apply the [interrupt working rules](../Interrupts/ATtiny162x_Working_Rules_Interrupts.md) whenever RTC or PIT interrupts are used, and apply the [GPIO working rules](../GPIO/ATtiny162x_Working_Rules_GPIO.md) when `TOSC1` or `TOSC2` is assigned to the RTC clock system.

### Define `F_CPU` only when required

RTC and PIT timing does not use `F_CPU`. Do not add an `F_CPU` definition solely because the program uses RTC or PIT.

Inspect the project source for an existing `F_CPU` definition only when another part of the program, a library facility, or a header requires it. If it exists, use its value and do not add a second definition. Ensure that the definition appears before any header that uses `F_CPU` during compilation.

If `F_CPU` is required, is not defined, and the program does not reconfigure CLKCTRL, the AI must explicitly inform the user that it proposes to assume the reset-default CPU frequency. The AI must state that, after the user accepts this assumption, it will add the following definition before the header files:

```c
#define F_CPU 3333333UL
```

The AI should use a clear notification such as:

> `F_CPU` is not defined. I propose to assume the reset-default CPU frequency of 3333333 Hz and add `#define F_CPU 3333333UL`.

Do not add this definition until the user accepts the proposed assumption. This assumption is permitted only when the program does not reconfigure the system clock through CLKCTRL and the definition is actually required by the program.

If the program requires `F_CPU` and changes the system clock through CLKCTRL, define `F_CPU` as the resulting CPU frequency instead of `3333333UL`. If the project contains conflicting `F_CPU` definitions, report the conflict rather than silently selecting one. Do not add conditional preprocessor directives merely to hide a conflict; inspect the relevant project sources and make the definition consistent with the actual clock configuration.

### Required headers

Always include the MPLAB XC8 top-level device header:

```c
#include <xc.h>
```

When RTC or PIT interrupts are used, also include the AVR interrupt header:

```c
#include <avr/interrupt.h>
```

## WR-RTC-02: Select the timing function and `CLK_RTC` source

### Select the required timing function

- For a simple periodic interrupt or wake-up, evaluate PIT first. Use PIT when one of its fixed periods satisfies the required timing and accuracy.
- Use the 16-bit RTC counter when PIT cannot provide the required period or accuracy, or when the application requires `CNT`, `PER`, `CMP`, overflow, or compare-match operation.
- Use PIT for a divided-clock event. Prefer PIT for periodic wake-up when especially low energy consumption is required, because PIT continues operating in every sleep mode and can therefore be used in deeper sleep modes than the RTC counter function.
- RTC and PIT can operate at the same time, but they share `CLK_RTC`, the prescaler, and its phase. Account for this shared state when configuring or starting either function.

The actual energy consumption depends on the selected `CLK_RTC` source, sleep mode, and every other enabled peripheral. Do not claim a specific power saving without checking the complete device configuration and the applicable electrical data.

### Select and prepare `CLK_RTC`

RTC and PIT share one `CLK_RTC` source. Select that source before calculating any RTC or PIT period or enabling either timing function. The available selections are the internal 32.768 kHz oscillator (`INT32K`), the internal 1.024 kHz oscillator (`INT1K`), the 32.768 kHz crystal oscillator (`TOSC32K`), and an external clock applied through TOSC1 (`EXTCLK`).

For primary initialization after reset, `RTC.CLKSEL` already selects `INT32K`. Do not write the same selection only to reproduce the verified reset value. If the clock selection might have been changed or the peripheral is being reconfigured, select the required source explicitly.

Before selecting `TOSC32K` or `EXTCLK` in `RTC.CLKSEL`, configure and enable XOSC32K through CLKCTRL and ensure that the selected source is ready for use. Configure `SEL` and `RUNSTDBY` for the required clock type and sleep behavior. For a crystal or external clock, also verify the TOSC1/TOSC2 pin use, board connections, and required external circuitry.

The RTC materials do not yet define the complete CLKCTRL register sequence, source-ready indication, start-up timing, or electrical design. Do not invent that code from the RTC chapter; obtain it from the applicable CLKCTRL and electrical documentation before generating a `TOSC32K` or `EXTCLK` implementation.

Base every timing calculation on the actual frequency and accuracy of the selected source rather than only its nominal source name. If software reads `RTC.CNT`, ensure that `CLK_PER` is at least four times faster than `CLK_RTC`. This constraint applies regardless of the RTC prescaler setting.

## WR-RTC-03: Synchronize RTC register access

RTC and PIT operate in the `CLK_RTC` clock domain, which is asynchronous to the peripheral clock domain. Writes to synchronized registers do not necessarily take effect immediately. Before writing a synchronized register, wait until the corresponding busy flag is cleared. Do not replace this check with a fixed software delay.

Use the following register-to-busy-flag relationships:

- before writing `RTC.CTRLA`, wait for `RTC.STATUS & RTC_CTRLABUSY_bm` to become zero;
- before writing `RTC.CNT`, wait for `RTC.STATUS & RTC_CNTBUSY_bm` to become zero;
- before writing `RTC.PER`, wait for `RTC.STATUS & RTC_PERBUSY_bm` to become zero;
- before writing `RTC.CMP`, wait for `RTC.STATUS & RTC_CMPBUSY_bm` to become zero;
- before writing `RTC.PITCTRLA`, wait for `RTC.PITSTATUS & RTC_CTRLBUSY_bm` to become zero.

Use a register-specific wait immediately before each write. For example:

```c
while ((RTC.STATUS & RTC_CTRLABUSY_bm) != 0u) {}
RTC.CTRLA = /* required value */;
while ((RTC.STATUS & RTC_CTRLABUSY_bm) != 0u) {}
```

For PIT control, use its separate status register:

```c
while ((RTC.PITSTATUS & RTC_CTRLBUSY_bm) != 0u) {}
RTC.PITCTRLA = /* required value */;
while ((RTC.PITSTATUS & RTC_CTRLBUSY_bm) != 0u) {}
```

After a synchronized write, wait for the same busy flag to clear before another write to that register or before an operation that depends on the completed update. A following register-specific wait may provide this confirmation when the next operation uses the same synchronized register.

If a busy flag does not clear, do not bypass the check. Verify that the selected `CLK_RTC` source is running and that its clock configuration is valid.

### Protect 16-bit RTC register access

`RTC.CNT`, `RTC.PER`, and `RTC.CMP` are 16-bit register pairs that share `RTC.TEMP` for byte-wise CPU access. Use the 16-bit register members supplied by the selected device header rather than manually inventing register addresses or byte order. For example, use `RTC.PER = value;` only after the applicable busy flag has cleared.

Before accepting code as production-ready, verify that the selected MPLAB XC8 version emits the access sequence required by the device for each 16-bit read or write. The current local RTC chapter summary does not by itself establish the complete byte-order and temporary-register access rules.

An interrupt between the byte operations of a 16-bit RTC access can interfere if that ISR accesses any of `RTC.CNT`, `RTC.PER`, or `RTC.CMP`, because those registers share `RTC.TEMP`. When such concurrent access is possible, protect the complete 16-bit operation by saving `SREG`, calling `cli()`, performing the access, and restoring the saved `SREG`. A separate critical section is not required during one-time initialization before global interrupts are enabled, provided that no higher-priority or non-maskable context can access those registers.

Before reading `RTC.CNT`, also satisfy the requirement that `CLK_PER` be at least four times faster than `CLK_RTC`. Do not claim that a 16-bit access is atomic or compiler-verified without checking the selected device and toolchain configuration.

## WR-RTC-04: Configure timing

Obtain the required timer period or timer frequency from the user before calculating the RTC or PIT configuration. The user may specify a period in seconds, milliseconds, or microseconds. This target value is mandatory; do not continue with timer configuration when neither a target period nor a target frequency is known.

Ask the user for the permitted timing error. The tolerance may be stated as a percentage, a fractional error, an absolute time error, an absolute frequency error, or another unambiguous limit. If the user cannot provide a tolerance, select the configuration with the smallest attainable calculation error under the other established requirements and state that decision explicitly.

Do not use `F_CPU` to calculate an RTC or PIT period. These timing functions use `CLK_RTC`, not the CPU clock. Handle `F_CPU` only when it is required as specified under **Define `F_CPU` only when required**. Changing `F_CPU` cannot improve the RTC or PIT timing resolution or division accuracy. A CPU or peripheral clock change is relevant here only if it is necessary to satisfy the requirement that `CLK_PER` be at least four times faster than `CLK_RTC` when software reads `RTC.CNT`.

If the `CLK_RTC` source has not been specified, propose a source to the user and explain the choice. First consider the currently selected source; for primary initialization after reset, this is `INT32K`. Use it when it provides the required range and tolerance without unnecessary clock reconfiguration. A lower-frequency source can extend the available time range, but it also produces coarser timing resolution. Do not select the lowest frequency unconditionally.

### Calculate RTC counter timing

Calculate the RTC counter tick from the actual `CLK_RTC` frequency and the selected prescaler divisor:

```text
RTC tick period = PRESCALER / f_CLK_RTC
```

For a counter that starts at zero and overflows after counting through `RTC.PER`, calculate:

```text
number of counter ticks = required period x f_CLK_RTC / PRESCALER
RTC.PER = number of counter ticks - 1
```

The resulting RTC period and frequency are:

```text
T_actual = PRESCALER x (RTC.PER + 1) / f_CLK_RTC
f_actual = f_CLK_RTC / (PRESCALER x (RTC.PER + 1))
```

`RTC.PER` is a 16-bit register. Select the source and prescaler so that the rounded number of counter ticks is from 1 through 65536 and the resulting `RTC.PER` is from 0 through 65535. If several configurations satisfy the established requirements, normally prefer the smallest prescaler that permits the value to fit. This gives the finest counter resolution and usually the smallest attainable rounding error.

Round a non-integer tick count according to the required timing objective; normally use the nearest integer. Calculate the resulting period or frequency and verify it against the user's tolerance. A larger `RTC.PER + 1` provides finer relative adjustment, but it does not improve a result that is already exact.

If compare operation is used, verify that `RTC.CMP` fits in 16 bits. For a compare match intended to occur within the configured counter cycle, use a value that does not exceed `RTC.PER`. If timing must start from a known counter position, ensure that `RTC.CNT` has that value, normally zero. During primary initialization after reset, do not write zero solely to reproduce the verified reset value. When the counter may have run or the peripheral is being reconfigured, wait for `RTC_CNTBUSY_bm` to clear and write the required value explicitly. Observe the synchronization and 16-bit access rules before writing `RTC.CNT`, `RTC.PER`, or `RTC.CMP`.

Place the formula that calculates the `RTC.PER` register value in a named macro definition in the C source. Do not replace the formula with an unexplained numeric value. Use names that identify the quantities and their units, use integer suffixes such as `UL` where required, and verify that no intermediate calculation overflows its C integer type. For example, for a target expressed in milliseconds:

```c
#define RTC_CLOCK_HZ              32768UL
#define RTC_PRESCALER_DIV         1UL
#define RTC_TARGET_PERIOD_MS      1000UL
#define RTC_PERIOD_DENOMINATOR    (1000UL * RTC_PRESCALER_DIV)
#define RTC_COUNTER_TICKS         \
    ((RTC_CLOCK_HZ * RTC_TARGET_PERIOD_MS + \
      (RTC_PERIOD_DENOMINATOR / 2UL)) / RTC_PERIOD_DENOMINATOR)
#define RTC_PER_VALUE             (RTC_COUNTER_TICKS - 1UL)
```

Use the calculated macro when a `RTC.PER` write is required:

```c
RTC.PER = RTC_PER_VALUE;
```

Adapt the formula and unit-bearing macro names when the target is specified in seconds or microseconds. Confirm before generating the program that `RTC_COUNTER_TICKS` is from 1 through 65536 and that `RTC_PER_VALUE` is from 0 through 65535.

### Select PIT timing

PIT does not accept an arbitrary numeric period value. Select one of the XC8 period constants from `RTC_PERIOD_CYC4_gc` through `RTC_PERIOD_CYC32768_gc`. `RTC_PERIOD_OFF_gc` does not define an operating period, and the reserved field value must not be used.

Calculate the PIT period from the selected number of `CLK_RTC` cycles:

```text
T_actual = selected CLK_RTC cycles / f_CLK_RTC
```

Choose an exact supported period when possible. Otherwise choose the supported value that best satisfies the established objective, calculate its error, and verify it against the user's tolerance. Use the synchronization rule for `RTC.PITCTRLA` before writing the selected period.

The first RTC counter tick or PIT periodic interrupt condition after enabling is not guaranteed to occur after one complete selected period because RTC and PIT share the running prescaler and its phase. Do not rely on the first interval being complete. Subsequent PIT periodic interrupt intervals during continuous operation have the selected period. Treat the divided-clock Event System outputs separately; they are level outputs from defined prescaler taps, not the `PI` interrupt condition selected by `RTC.PITCTRLA.PERIOD`.

### Report the timing decision

Before presenting or generating the final program, inform the user of:

- the requested period and frequency;
- the actual calculated period and frequency;
- the absolute and relative calculation error and whether it satisfies the requested tolerance;
- the selected `CLK_RTC` source and the frequency used in the calculation;
- the selected RTC prescaler and `RTC.PER` value, and `RTC.CMP` when used;
- the selected PIT `PERIOD` constant when PIT is used;
- any required assumption made about `F_CPU`, reported separately from the RTC timing calculation;
- any relevant first-interval limitation.

Calculation error caused by integer division is not the same as the physical frequency error of the selected clock source. If the source accuracy and stability are unknown, report only the mathematical configuration error and explicitly state that the total real-time accuracy cannot be guaranteed from the available information.

If no supported RTC or PIT configuration satisfies the requirements, inform the user and propose an applicable alternative: another prescaler, another `CLK_RTC` source, software counting of multiple timer periods, a relaxed tolerance, or a different timer peripheral. Do not propose a higher `F_CPU` as a way to improve RTC or PIT timing accuracy.

## WR-RTC-05: Configure interrupts, polling, or events

Decide how the application will receive the RTC or PIT result before enabling either timing function. Select one or more of the following mechanisms according to the application requirements:

- polling an interrupt flag without enabling the corresponding interrupt;
- an RTC or PIT interrupt;
- an Event System output;
- both an interrupt and an event when both consumers are required.

Do not enable an interrupt or configure an event route that the application does not use.

### Configure RTC counter interrupts

The RTC counter provides two interrupt sources:

- overflow (`OVF`), enabled with `RTC_OVF_bm` in `RTC.INTCTRL`;
- compare match (`CMP`), enabled with `RTC_CMP_bm` in `RTC.INTCTRL`.

Enable only the required source or sources. Use direct assignment during primary initialization so that the enabled set is explicit:

```c
RTC.INTCTRL = RTC_OVF_bm;
```

```c
RTC.INTCTRL = RTC_CMP_bm;
```

```c
RTC.INTCTRL = RTC_OVF_bm | RTC_CMP_bm;
```

Both RTC counter sources use the shared XC8 vector `RTC_CNT_vect`. If both sources are enabled, the ISR must read the relevant bits in `RTC.INTFLAGS`, service every asserted enabled source, and clear each serviced flag using write-one-to-clear semantics. If exactly one source is enabled and the program guarantees that this remains true, the ISR may directly service and clear that known source without dispatching on both flags.

Do not enable an RTC counter interrupt unless the program provides the corresponding `ISR(RTC_CNT_vect)` handler. Enabling a bit in `RTC.INTCTRL` does not start the RTC counter; `RTC.CTRLA.RTCEN` is handled separately under **Start RTC or PIT**.

### Configure the PIT interrupt

PIT provides the periodic interrupt source `PI`. Enable it with direct assignment during primary initialization:

```c
RTC.PITINTCTRL = RTC_PI_bm;
```

PIT uses the separate XC8 vector `RTC_PIT_vect` and the `PI` flag in `RTC.PITINTFLAGS`. Do not enable the PIT interrupt unless the program provides an `ISR(RTC_PIT_vect)` handler. Enabling `RTC_PI_bm` does not start PIT; `RTC.PITCTRLA.PITEN` is handled separately under **Start RTC or PIT**.

### Use polling when no interrupt is required

When the application polls a flag, leave its interrupt-enable bit cleared. Poll the required bit in `RTC.INTFLAGS` or `RTC.PITINTFLAGS`, perform the required action, and acknowledge the serviced condition with a direct write-one-to-clear operation. Do not call `sei()` solely for a polled RTC or PIT condition.

### Configure Event System use

The available RTC-related event generators are:

- `OVF`, a one-`CLK_RTC`-period pulse produced by RTC counter overflow;
- `CMP`, a one-`CLK_RTC`-period pulse produced by RTC compare match;
- `PIT_DIV64`, `PIT_DIV128`, `PIT_DIV256`, `PIT_DIV512`, `PIT_DIV1024`, `PIT_DIV2048`, `PIT_DIV4096`, and `PIT_DIV8192`, which are divided-clock level outputs.

Select the required generator, configure the EVSYS channel, and connect the required EVSYS user before relying on the event path. An RTC or PIT interrupt-enable bit is not required merely to generate an event. Enable the interrupt as well only when CPU service is also required.

The current RTC materials identify the available event outputs but do not define the EVSYS channel and user configuration. Do not invent EVSYS register settings or C code from the RTC information alone. Obtain and process the applicable EVSYS materials before generating a complete event-routing implementation.

### Preserve initialization order

Complete the required timing and interrupt or event configuration before starting RTC or PIT. Clear any applicable pending interrupt flags as described in WR-RTC-06, then start the selected timing function. If interrupts are used during primary initialization, enable global interrupts only after the complete peripheral initialization, immediately before the main `while (1)` loop.

Use the following general order:

```text
Configure timing
-> Configure the interrupt or event path
-> Clear applicable pending flags
-> Start RTC or PIT
-> Enable global interrupts when interrupts are used
```

For repeated initialization or runtime reconfiguration, apply the complete sequence in WR-RTC-11 instead of reusing this primary-initialization sequence without review.

## WR-RTC-06: Clear pending interrupt flags when required

Before starting RTC or PIT or relying on a newly enabled interrupt, clear the applicable pending flag if the timing function may have operated previously or the flag state is otherwise not guaranteed. A separate clear is not required during primary initialization after reset when the reset value is known, the timing function has not run, and no flag could have been set.

RTC and PIT interrupt flags use write-one-to-clear semantics. Clear only the intended flags by direct assignment. Do not use a read-modify-write operation such as `|=`.

Clear the RTC overflow flag with:

```c
RTC.INTFLAGS = RTC_OVF_bm;
```

Clear the RTC compare-match flag with:

```c
RTC.INTFLAGS = RTC_CMP_bm;
```

When both RTC counter sources are used and both pending conditions are to be discarded, clear both flags with one write:

```c
RTC.INTFLAGS = RTC_OVF_bm | RTC_CMP_bm;
```

Clear the PIT periodic interrupt flag with:

```c
RTC.PITINTFLAGS = RTC_PI_bm;
```

## WR-RTC-07: Configure crystal frequency correction when required

Frequency correction is optional. Do not enable it unless the application has an externally established correction value. `RTC.CALIB.ERROR` accepts a magnitude from 0 through 127, corresponding to one-PPM steps, and `RTC.CALIB.SIGN` selects the correction direction:

- `SIGN = 0` applies positive correction and makes the prescaler count slower;
- `SIGN = 1` applies negative correction and makes the prescaler count faster.

Negative correction requires the RTC counter prescaler to be at least `DIV2`. Reject a configuration that requests negative correction with `DIV1`. The correction affects the shared prescaler and therefore affects both RTC counter timing and PIT timing.

Write the established magnitude and sign to `RTC.CALIB` before enabling `RTC_CORREN_bm` in `RTC.CTRLA`. Use the device-header masks `RTC_ERROR_gm` and `RTC_SIGN_bm`; validate the magnitude before converting it to `uint8_t`. Do not invent a calibration value or infer one only from the nominal oscillator name.

When correction is enabled, distinguish the integer configuration error from the physical clock correction and the remaining oscillator error. Include the applied correction in the reported timing assumptions. Disabling `RTC_CORREN_bm` does not necessarily stop an active correction cycle immediately; the current correction cycle completes before correction stops.

If no measured correction is required during primary initialization, leave `RTC.CALIB` and `CORREN` at their verified reset values instead of writing zero solely to reproduce those values.

## WR-RTC-08: Start RTC or PIT

Start RTC or PIT only after completing the required clock, timing, interrupt or event, and pending-flag configuration.

### Start the RTC counter

Before writing `RTC.CTRLA`, wait for `RTC_CTRLABUSY_bm` to clear. During primary initialization, write the selected prescaler, every required optional control bit, and `RTC_RTCEN_bm` together so that the complete configuration is explicit. For example, when the calculation selected `DIV32` and neither Standby operation nor frequency correction is required:

```c
while ((RTC.STATUS & RTC_CTRLABUSY_bm) != 0u) {}
RTC.CTRLA = RTC_PRESCALER_DIV32_gc
           | RTC_RTCEN_bm;
while ((RTC.STATUS & RTC_CTRLABUSY_bm) != 0u) {}
```

The specific prescaler constant in the program must be the result of the timing calculation; `RTC_PRESCALER_DIV32_gc` above is only an example. Include `RTC_RUNSTDBY_bm` when the RTC counter must continue in Standby. Include `RTC_CORREN_bm` only after applying WR-RTC-07, writing the established calibration value, and verifying the negative-correction prescaler restriction when applicable.

Do not write only `RTC_RTCEN_bm` when a non-default prescaler, `RUNSTDBY`, or `CORREN` is required, because direct assignment replaces every field in `RTC.CTRLA`. A value containing only `RTC_RTCEN_bm` is valid only when `DIV1` and the reset state of every optional field are intentionally required.

### Start PIT

Before writing `RTC.PITCTRLA`, wait for `RTC_CTRLBUSY_bm` in `RTC.PITSTATUS` to clear. During primary initialization, write the selected `PERIOD` value and `RTC_PITEN_bm` together. For example, when the timing decision selected 1024 `CLK_RTC` cycles:

```c
while ((RTC.PITSTATUS & RTC_CTRLBUSY_bm) != 0u) {}
RTC.PITCTRLA = RTC_PERIOD_CYC1024_gc
              | RTC_PITEN_bm;
while ((RTC.PITSTATUS & RTC_CTRLBUSY_bm) != 0u) {}
```

The specific `RTC_PERIOD_CYC..._gc` constant must be the result of the PIT timing selection; `RTC_PERIOD_CYC1024_gc` above is only an example. Do not write only `RTC_PITEN_bm`, because direct assignment would select `RTC_PERIOD_OFF_gc` and discard the required `PERIOD` field.

After either synchronized control-register write, wait for the corresponding busy flag to clear before performing an operation that depends on the completed update.

RTC and PIT are enabled independently and may operate at the same time. They share the prescaler and its phase, so sequential software writes cannot guarantee a common zero-phase start or a complete first interval.

### Event System does not start RTC or PIT

RTC and PIT provide Event System generator outputs; the available RTC materials do not define an Event System input that starts either timing function. EVSYS routing therefore does not replace setting `RTC_RTCEN_bm` or `RTC_PITEN_bm`.

The shared prescaler runs when either `RTCEN` or `PITEN` is set. Enable the timing function required to produce the selected RTC or divided-clock event, then use EVSYS to route that generated signal to its consumer.

## WR-RTC-09: Enable global interrupts when used

When RTC or PIT interrupts are used during primary initialization, call `sei()` only after completing the clock, timing, peripheral interrupt, pending-flag, and start configuration. Ensure that the program provides every required ISR before enabling global interrupt handling. Place `sei()` immediately before the main `while (1)` loop.

```c
int main(void)
{
    /* Configure CLK_RTC. */
    /* Configure RTC or PIT timing. */
    /* Configure the required peripheral interrupt. */
    /* Clear any applicable pending interrupt flag. */
    /* Start RTC or PIT. */

    sei();

    while (1)
    {
        /* Main application loop. */
    }
}
```

`sei()` enables global interrupt handling; it does not replace enabling the required peripheral source in `RTC.INTCTRL` or `RTC.PITINTCTRL`. Do not call `sei()` solely for flag polling or Event System operation.

For temporary interrupt suppression during later reconfiguration, follow the project interrupt working rules for `cli()` and for saving and restoring the previous `SREG` state. Do not duplicate those general interrupt-control rules here.

## WR-RTC-10: Handle RTC and PIT operation

Apply the general ISR, shared-data, atomic-access, and interrupt-state rules from [ATtiny162x_Working_Rules_Interrupts.md](../Interrupts/ATtiny162x_Working_Rules_Interrupts.md). Clear each serviced RTC or PIT flag before performing the corresponding application action. Keep every ISR short and bounded; normally move lengthy processing to the main loop.

Software delays inside an ISR are not prohibited, but they are discouraged. Use one only when it is short, bounded, justified by the application, and verified not to cause unacceptable interrupt latency or missed events.

### Handle a PIT interrupt directly

PIT has one interrupt source and a dedicated vector. Clear its flag by direct write before the application action:

```c
ISR(RTC_PIT_vect)
{
    RTC.PITINTFLAGS = RTC_PI_bm;

    /* Short application action. */
}
```

### Defer PIT processing to the main loop

Declare data shared between an ISR and the main program as `volatile`. Use a counter rather than a Boolean flag when more than one event may occur before the main loop processes it. Select sufficient counter capacity and define the required overflow behavior for the application. The following example uses saturation: once the counter reaches `UINT8_MAX`, further PIT occurrences are coalesced until the main loop consumes an event.

```c
volatile uint8_t pit_event_count = 0u;

ISR(RTC_PIT_vect)
{
    RTC.PITINTFLAGS = RTC_PI_bm;

    if (pit_event_count != UINT8_MAX)
    {
        pit_event_count++;
    }
}
```

`UINT8_MAX` is available through `<stdint.h>`, which is included by the selected device header used through `<xc.h>`. If the application must detect that saturation occurred, add a separate overflow indication or use a wider counter and apply the corresponding atomic-access rules.

Access the shared counter atomically. Preserve and restore the previous global interrupt state rather than calling `sei()` unconditionally:

```c
while (1)
{
    uint8_t process_event = 0u;
    uint8_t saved_sreg = SREG;

    cli();

    if (pit_event_count != 0u)
    {
        pit_event_count--;
        process_event = 1u;
    }

    SREG = saved_sreg;

    if (process_event != 0u)
    {
        /* Process one PIT interrupt occurrence outside the critical section. */
    }
}
```

Keep the protected section limited to the shared-data operation. Perform the lengthy application work after restoring the previous interrupt state.

### Handle one RTC counter interrupt source

When exactly one RTC counter interrupt source is enabled and the program guarantees that this remains true, the ISR may directly clear and service that known source without reading `RTC.INTFLAGS`. For an overflow-only configuration:

```c
ISR(RTC_CNT_vect)
{
    RTC.INTFLAGS = RTC_OVF_bm;

    /* Short overflow action. */
}
```

Use the corresponding direct `RTC_CMP_bm` write for a compare-only configuration.

### Handle both RTC counter interrupt sources

When both `OVF` and `CMP` are enabled, snapshot the shared flag register, clear only the captured relevant flags, and service every captured source:

```c
ISR(RTC_CNT_vect)
{
    uint8_t flags = RTC.INTFLAGS;

    RTC.INTFLAGS = flags & (RTC_OVF_bm | RTC_CMP_bm);

    if ((flags & RTC_OVF_bm) != 0u)
    {
        /* Short overflow action. */
    }

    if ((flags & RTC_CMP_bm) != 0u)
    {
        /* Short compare-match action. */
    }
}
```

This example gives `OVF` application processing priority over `CMP` when both flags were captured together. Reverse the order when the application requires the opposite priority, and state the selected simultaneous-event policy explicitly.

### Poll without interrupts

When polling is selected, leave the corresponding peripheral interrupt enable cleared. Test and acknowledge the flag in the main loop; global interrupt enable is not required for this operation. For PIT:

```c
while (1)
{
    if ((RTC.PITINTFLAGS & RTC_PI_bm) != 0u)
    {
        RTC.PITINTFLAGS = RTC_PI_bm;

        /* Process the PIT interrupt occurrence. */
    }
}
```

When RTC or PIT is used only as an Event System generator and no CPU action is required, no RTC or PIT ISR is necessary.

## WR-RTC-11: Stop and reconfigure RTC or PIT safely

Treat repeated initialization as a separate operation from primary initialization after reset. Do not assume reset values during repeated initialization, and do not change a running timing configuration without defining how the current interval, pending flags, and application state are handled.

Before reconfiguration while interrupts may already be enabled:

1. Decide whether pending RTC or PIT conditions must be processed or discarded.
2. Prevent the affected ISR from observing a partial configuration. Preserve and restore the previous global interrupt state as specified by the interrupt working rules, or disable only the affected peripheral interrupt source when that narrower method is sufficient. Preserve unrelated interrupt-enable bits.
3. Stop each affected timing function by clearing its enable bit through a complete, intentional control-register value. Wait for `RTC_CTRLABUSY_bm` or `RTC_CTRLBUSY_bm` to clear after the control write before depending on the stopped state.
4. If `CLK_RTC`, XOSC32K configuration, or shared frequency correction will change, coordinate both RTC and PIT. Do not change a shared clock assumption while the other function continues to rely on it.
5. Write the new `CALIB`, `CNT`, `PER`, `CMP`, prescaler, or PIT period values as required, applying the register-specific synchronization and 16-bit access rules. Do not rewrite values that are intentionally preserved.
6. Clear only the pending flags that the reconfiguration policy has chosen to discard. Use direct write-one-to-clear assignments.
7. Restore the required peripheral interrupt enables, start the required timing functions, wait for synchronized control writes to complete, and only then restore the previous global interrupt state.

Stopping RTC or PIT does not guarantee a new zero-phase start of the shared prescaler. The prescaler runs while either `RTCEN` or `PITEN` is set, and sequential writes cannot synchronize the two functions to a common phase. After restart, retain the first-interval limitation unless a separately verified hardware procedure establishes the required phase.

When only one of RTC or PIT is reconfigured while the other remains active, account for the continuing shared-prescaler phase. Changing `CLK_RTC` or enabling or changing frequency correction affects both timing functions and therefore requires review of both configurations.

## WR-RTC-12: Define sleep and debug behavior

### Account for sleep operation

PIT can operate in every sleep mode. The RTC counter operates in Idle and can operate in Standby when `RTC_RUNSTDBY_bm` is set. Confirm that the selected `CLK_RTC` source also remains available in the required sleep mode.

Sleep-mode selection and entry require SLPCTRL information that is outside the current RTC materials. Do not invent SLPCTRL configuration code from the RTC information alone; obtain and process the applicable sleep-controller materials before generating a complete sleep implementation.

### Account for Break Debug operation

Choose whether RTC and PIT must continue while the CPU is halted by the debugger:

- with `RTC.DBGCTRL.DBGRUN = 0`, RTC halts and ignores incoming events during Break Debug;
- with `RTC.DBGCTRL.DBGRUN = 1`, RTC continues operating;
- with `RTC.PITDBGCTRL.DBGRUN = 0`, the PIT output is forced low during Break Debug;
- with `RTC.PITDBGCTRL.DBGRUN = 1`, PIT continues operating.

If the PIT output was high when the CPU halted while `RTC.PITDBGCTRL.DBGRUN` was zero, resuming execution can create a new positive edge and set `PI`. Treat that possible extra PIT condition as debugger-induced behavior; do not interpret it as ordinary uninterrupted timing.

During primary initialization, leave the debug-control register at its verified reset value when halting RTC or PIT during Break Debug is intended. When continued operation is required, use an explicit assignment:

```c
RTC.DBGCTRL = RTC_DBGRUN_bm;
RTC.PITDBGCTRL = RTC_DBGRUN_bm;
```

Report the selected sleep and debug behavior with the timing configuration. Debug-control settings do not replace `RTCEN`, `PITEN`, or `RUNSTDBY`.

# ATtiny1624/1626/1627 TCA - 16-bit Timer/Counter Type A

## 1. Purpose and source

This device-specific reference is derived from chapter 21, "TCA - 16-bit Timer/Counter Type A," printed pages 194-242 of `../ATtiny1624-26-27-DataSheet-DS40002234B.pdf`, revision DS40002234B (2021). PDF and printed page numbers are the same for this range. The chapter was checked from extracted text and rendered pages.

This preliminary file summarizes only chapter 21. It does not select physical pins, configure PORT or PORTMUX, route Event System channels, define compiler-specific C symbols, provide tested drivers, or incorporate errata.

## 2. Peripheral structure

In Normal mode, TCA contains one 16-bit base counter, one 16-bit period register, three compare channels, double-buffered period and compare values, control logic, and waveform generation. `CLK_TCA` can come from prescaled `CLK_PER` or from Event System activity. [pp. 194-196]

In Split mode, the same peripheral becomes two independent 8-bit down-counters. Each counter has its own period and three compare values, providing up to six waveform outputs. Split mode changes the meaning and width of several registers. See the derived [Normal-mode block diagram](ATtiny162x_TCA_Block_Diagram.svg) and [Split-mode diagram](ATtiny162x_TCA_Split_Mode.svg).

The external TCA signals are waveform outputs named `WOn`. Physical pins and alternate routes are defined outside chapter 21.

## 3. Terms and timing points

The chapter uses these definitions: [p. 196]

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `BOTTOM` | Counter value becomes `0x0000` in Normal mode, or zero for an 8-bit Split counter |
| `MAX` | Counter becomes all ones |
| `TOP` | Highest value in the selected count sequence |
| `UPDATE` | Buffered values are transferred at BOTTOM or TOP as selected by `WGMODE`, unless `LUPD` blocks the transfer |
| `CNT` | Counter value |
| `CMPn` | Compare value for channel n |
| `PER` | Period value |

An interrupt request, event, or waveform change caused by reaching TOP, BOTTOM, or `CMPn` occurs on the next `CLK_TCA` cycle after the triggering condition. [p. 196]

## 4. Clock and basic initialization

`CTRLA.CLKSEL` selects `CLK_PER` divided by 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 64, 256, or 1024. With prescaler divisor `N`:

```text
f_TCA = f_CLK_PER / N
```

Basic Normal-mode initialization is: [p. 197]

1. Write the TOP value to `TCAn.PER`.
2. Select the prescaler in `TCAn.CTRLA.CLKSEL` as required.
3. Optionally configure event operation in `TCAn.EVCTRL`.
4. Set `TCAn.CTRLA.ENABLE`.
5. Read the current counter value from `TCAn.CNT` when required.

The source lists selection of `CLKSEL` implicitly through the enable step rather than as a separate numbered step. For deterministic code, configure every required field before setting `ENABLE`.

## 5. Normal-mode count behavior

In Normal waveform mode, `CTRLE.DIR` selects up-counting or down-counting. [p. 197]

- While counting up, the counter reaches `PER` (TOP) and wraps to zero on the next timer tick.
- While counting down, reaching BOTTOM causes the counter to reload from `PER`.
- A CPU or UPDI write to `CNT` has priority over count, clear, or reload and takes effect immediately.
- Software may change `DIR` while the counter is running, subject to the selected waveform mode and any event action controlling direction.

## 6. Waveform generation modes

`CTRLB.WGMODE` controls count sequence, TOP, UPDATE, and overflow/underflow flag timing. [p. 210]

| Value | Name | Operation | TOP | UPDATE | `OVF` condition |
|---:|---|---|---|---|---|
| `0x0` | `NORMAL` | Normal counter | `PER` | TOP when counting up | TOP when counting up |
| `0x1` | `FRQ` | Frequency generation | `CMP0` | TOP when counting up | TOP when counting up |
| `0x2` | - | Reserved | - | - | - |
| `0x3` | `SINGLESLOPE` | Single-slope PWM | `PER` | BOTTOM | BOTTOM |
| `0x4` | - | Reserved | - | - | - |
| `0x5` | `DSTOP` | Dual-slope PWM | `PER` | BOTTOM | TOP |
| `0x6` | `DSBOTH` | Dual-slope PWM | `PER` | BOTTOM | TOP and BOTTOM |
| `0x7` | `DSBOTTOM` | Dual-slope PWM | `PER` | BOTTOM | BOTTOM |

The three dual-slope selections have the same PWM waveform rule and differ in the condition that sets `OVF`.

## 7. Double buffering

`PER` and `CMP0` through `CMP2` have corresponding buffers `PERBUF` and `CMP0BUF` through `CMP2BUF`. Writing a buffer sets its Buffer Valid flag (`PERBV` or `CMPnBV`). At the mode-specific UPDATE condition, valid buffered values transfer to the active registers and their valid flags clear. The new `CMPn` value is used for comparison from the next count. [pp. 197-199]

Direct writes to `PER` or `CMPn` bypass buffering. A direct period write takes effect immediately. If a new `PER` value is below the current up-counting `CNT`, the next equality with TOP has already been missed and the counter can wrap through MAX before reaching the new TOP. In PWM operation this may produce an abnormally long cycle or irregular waveform. Writing `PERBUF` and `CMPnBUF` avoids this condition by transferring values at UPDATE. See the derived [double-buffering diagram](ATtiny162x_TCA_Double_Buffering.svg).

### 7.1. Locking coordinated updates

`CTRLE.LUPD = 1` blocks normal UPDATE transfers even when an UPDATE condition occurs. An explicit `CMD = UPDATE` is not blocked by `LUPD`.

`CTRLB.ALUPD = 1` automatically coordinates enabled compare channels:

1. Hardware sets `LUPD`.
2. Software writes every enabled `CMPnBUF`.
3. When all enabled compare-channel Buffer Valid flags are set, hardware clears `LUPD`.
4. At the next UPDATE condition, valid buffer values transfer to active registers.
5. Hardware sets `LUPD` again for the next group.

The ALUPD release condition is based on enabled compare-channel valid flags. The chapter does not include `PERBV` in that release condition.

## 8. Compare channels and output routing

Each channel continuously compares `CNT` with `CMPn`. Equality produces a match; the corresponding flag and optional event or waveform action occur on the next timer clock. `CMPnBUF` supplies a synchronized, glitch-reducing update path. [p. 199]

To make a waveform visible on a pin:

1. Select a non-Normal waveform mode in `CTRLB.WGMODE`.
2. Set the corresponding `CTRLB.CMPnEN` bit.
3. Select an alternate output route in PORTMUX if required.
4. Configure the selected PORT pin as an output.
5. Optionally use `PORTx.PINnCTRL.INVEN` to invert the waveform.

When a channel is enabled, TCA overrides the corresponding `PORTx.OUT` value. `CTRLC.CMPnOV` provides direct access to the internal waveform output value while TCA is disabled. For a physical pad, `CMPnEN` must still be set; a CCL connection bypasses the `CMPnEN` requirement. [pp. 202, 211]

## 9. Frequency generation

In `FRQ` mode, `CMP0` is TOP. WO0 toggles on each `CNT = CMP0` match, producing: [pp. 199-200]

```text
f_FRQ = f_CLK_PER / (2 * N * (CMP0 + 1))
```

The maximum is `f_CLK_PER / 2` with `CMP0 = 0` and `N = 1`. `CMP1` and `CMP2` can produce additional outputs that are identical to or phase-offset from WO0. The offset equations in the source apply only when `CMPn < CMP0`; the correct expression depends on count direction and the relationship between `CMPn` and the current `CNT`. Changing an unbuffered compare value at run time can miss a match or cause two matches in one waveform period.

## 10. Single-slope PWM

In `SINGLESLOPE` mode, `PER` is TOP. The counter counts from BOTTOM to TOP and then restarts at BOTTOM. Counting from TOP to BOTTOM is not supported in this mode. [p. 201]

- The waveform output is set at BOTTOM.
- It is cleared on `CNT = CMPn`.
- `CMPn = BOTTOM` produces static low.
- `CMPn > TOP` produces static high.

Resolution and frequency are:

```text
R_PWM_SS = log2(PER + 1)
f_PWM_SS = f_CLK_PER / (N * (PER + 1))
```

The documented resolution range is 2 bits at `PER = 0x0003` through 16 bits at `PER = 0xFFFF`.

## 11. Dual-slope PWM

In `DSTOP`, `DSBOTH`, or `DSBOTTOM`, the counter repeatedly counts BOTTOM to TOP and TOP to BOTTOM. [p. 202]

- The waveform output is set at BOTTOM.
- It is cleared on an up-counting compare match.
- It is set on a down-counting compare match.
- `CMPn = BOTTOM` produces static low.
- `CMPn = TOP` produces static high.

Resolution and frequency are:

```text
R_PWM_DS = log2(PER + 1)
f_PWM_DS = f_CLK_PER / (2 * N * PER)
```

Dual-slope PWM requires approximately twice as many counter steps per period and therefore has approximately half the maximum frequency of single-slope PWM. See the derived [waveform-mode diagram](ATtiny162x_TCA_Waveform_Modes.svg).

## 12. Timer commands

Write `CTRLESET.CMD` to issue an immediate command: [pp. 202-203, 213-214]

| Value | Name | Effect |
|---:|---|---|
| `0x0` | `NONE` | No command |
| `0x1` | `UPDATE` | Force buffered values to update; ignores `LUPD` |
| `0x2` | `RESTART` | Force restart; counter, direction, and compare outputs become zero |
| `0x3` | `RESET` | Hard reset; ignored while `ENABLE = 1` |

The command field always reads as zero. Disable TCA before issuing RESET.

`CTRLESET` and `CTRLECLR` provide write-one set and write-one clear access to `LUPD` and `DIR`, avoiding read-modify-write operations. `CTRLFSET` and `CTRLFCLR` provide the same access pattern for Buffer Valid bits.

## 13. Split mode

Set `CTRLD.SPLITM` to reinterpret TCA as two independent 8-bit timers: [pp. 203-204]

- Low timer: `LCNT`, `LPER`, `LCMP0` through `LCMP2`, outputs WO0 through WO2.
- High timer: `HCNT`, `HPER`, `HCMP0` through `HCMP2`, outputs WO3 through WO5.
- Both timers share `CTRLA.CLKSEL`, `CTRLA.ENABLE`, `RUNSTDBY`, and `DBGCTRL`.
- Both counters are down-counting only.
- Waveform generation is fixed to single-slope PWM behavior.
- Event-controlled operation is unavailable.
- Buffer registers and Buffer Valid flags are unavailable.
- Every active register is accessed as one byte.
- The low timer has compare interrupts; the high timer has no compare interrupt or compare flag.
- Both timers have underflow interrupts and events.

In Split PWM, the output is cleared at BOTTOM and set on compare match. Maximum duty cycle is `TOP / (TOP + 1)`.

### 13.1. Changing between Normal and Split modes

Changing `SPLITM` changes register meanings but does not clear existing values. The chapter recommends this transition sequence:

1. Clear `CTRLA.ENABLE`.
2. Issue a hard RESET command.
3. Select or clear `CTRLD.SPLITM` for the required mode.
4. Configure the new mode completely before re-enabling TCA.

In Split mode, `CMD` must be combined with `CMDEN = BOTH`; RESET requires both timers to be selected. UPDATE is reserved in Split mode.

### 13.2. Split-mode initialization

After the hard reset:

1. Set `CTRLD.SPLITM`.
2. Write `LPER` and `HPER`.
3. Write required `LCMPn` and `HCMPn` values and configure output enables.
4. Select the common clock prescaler.
5. Set `CTRLA.ENABLE`.
6. Read `LCNT` and `HCNT` independently when required.

## 14. Events

TCA event outputs are one-`CLK_PER`-period pulses. Event-generator conditions are identical to the conditions setting the corresponding interrupt flags. [pp. 205-206]

| Generator | Normal mode | Split mode |
|---|---|---|
| `OVF_LUNF` | Overflow | Low-timer underflow |
| `HUNF` | Not available | High-timer underflow |
| `CMP0_LCMP0` | Compare channel 0 match | Low-timer channel 0 match |
| `CMP1_LCMP1` | Compare channel 1 match | Low-timer channel 1 match |
| `CMP2_LCMP2` | Compare channel 2 match | Low-timer channel 2 match |

Normal mode has two synchronous event users:

- CNTA can count on a positive edge, count on any edge, count prescaled clock cycles while the level is high, or use the level for count direction.
- CNTB can use the level for count direction or restart on a positive edge, any edge, or while the level is high.

Set `EVCTRL.CNTAEI` or `CNTBEI` to enable the corresponding input and select the action with `EVACTA` or `EVACTB`. If both inputs control direction, their signals are ORed; both must be low for up-counting. Level-controlled event actions are reliable only when the event frequency is lower than the timer frequency. Event inputs are not used in Split mode.

## 15. Interrupts and flags

### 15.1. Normal mode

| Vector/flag | Condition |
|---|---|
| `OVF` | TOP or BOTTOM according to `WGMODE` |
| `CMP0` | `CNT = CMP0` |
| `CMP1` | `CNT = CMP1` |
| `CMP2` | `CNT = CMP2` |

### 15.2. Split mode

| Vector/flag | Condition |
|---|---|
| `LUNF` | Low counter reaches BOTTOM |
| `HUNF` | High counter reaches BOTTOM |
| `LCMP0` | `LCNT = LCMP0` |
| `LCMP1` | `LCNT = LCMP1` |
| `LCMP2` | `LCNT = LCMP2` |

Set the corresponding bit in `INTCTRL` to enable a source. Every flag in `INTFLAGS` is cleared by writing a one. The request remains active until its flag is cleared. CPUINT priority, ISR syntax, and global interrupt control are outside chapter 21.

## 16. Sleep and debug behavior

- TCA halts in Standby by default.
- Set `CTRLA.RUNSTDBY` to keep TCA fully operational in Standby.
- All TCA operation halts in Power-Down.
- With `DBGCTRL.DBGRUN = 0`, TCA halts in Break Debug mode and ignores events.
- With `DBGCTRL.DBGRUN = 1`, it continues while the CPU is halted.

## 17. Register summary - Normal mode

| Offset | Register | Reset | Key contents |
|---:|---|---:|---|
| `0x00` | `CTRLA` | `0x00` | `RUNSTDBY`, `CLKSEL`, `ENABLE` |
| `0x01` | `CTRLB` | `0x00` | `CMPnEN`, `ALUPD`, `WGMODE` |
| `0x02` | `CTRLC` | `0x00` | `CMPnOV` |
| `0x03` | `CTRLD` | `0x00` | `SPLITM` |
| `0x04` | `CTRLECLR` | `0x00` | `CMD`, `LUPD`, `DIR`; write-one clear view |
| `0x05` | `CTRLESET` | `0x00` | `CMD`, `LUPD`, `DIR`; write-one set view |
| `0x06` | `CTRLFCLR` | `0x00` | `CMPnBV`, `PERBV`; write-one clear view |
| `0x07` | `CTRLFSET` | `0x00` | `CMPnBV`, `PERBV`; write-one set view |
| `0x09` | `EVCTRL` | `0x00` | Event actions and enables |
| `0x0A` | `INTCTRL` | `0x00` | `CMP2`, `CMP1`, `CMP0`, `OVF` enables |
| `0x0B` | `INTFLAGS` | `0x00` | `CMP2`, `CMP1`, `CMP0`, `OVF` flags |
| `0x0E` | `DBGCTRL` | `0x00` | `DBGRUN` |
| `0x0F` | `TEMP` | `0x00` | Shared temporary byte for 16-bit access |
| `0x20` | `CNT` | `0x0000` | 16-bit counter |
| `0x26` | `PER` | `0xFFFF` | 16-bit TOP except in FRQ mode |
| `0x28`, `0x2A`, `0x2C` | `CMP0`, `CMP1`, `CMP2` | `0x0000` | Active compare values |
| `0x36` | `PERBUF` | `0xFFFF` | Buffered period |
| `0x38`, `0x3A`, `0x3C` | `CMP0BUF`, `CMP1BUF`, `CMP2BUF` | `0x0000` | Buffered compare values |

`CNT`, `PER`, `CMPn`, `PERBUF`, and `CMPnBUF` are 16-bit register pairs. They share `TEMP` for CPU single-cycle access. Exact read/write sequencing and atomicity rules are defined in the AVR CPU chapter, not chapter 21.

## 18. Register summary - Split mode

| Offset | Register | Reset | Key contents |
|---:|---|---:|---|
| `0x00` | `CTRLA` | `0x00` | Shared `RUNSTDBY`, `CLKSEL`, `ENABLE` |
| `0x01` | `CTRLB` | `0x00` | High and low compare-output enables |
| `0x02` | `CTRLC` | `0x00` | High and low compare-output values |
| `0x03` | `CTRLD` | `0x00` | `SPLITM` |
| `0x04` | `CTRLECLR` | `0x00` | `CMD`, `CMDEN`; write-one clear view |
| `0x05` | `CTRLESET` | `0x00` | `CMD`, `CMDEN`; write-one set view |
| `0x0A` | `INTCTRL` | `0x00` | `LCMP2:0`, `HUNF`, `LUNF` enables |
| `0x0B` | `INTFLAGS` | `0x00` | `LCMP2:0`, `HUNF`, `LUNF` flags |
| `0x0E` | `DBGCTRL` | `0x00` | `DBGRUN` |
| `0x20` | `LCNT` | `0x00` | Low-timer counter |
| `0x21` | `HCNT` | `0x00` | High-timer counter |
| `0x26` | `LPER` | `0xFF` | Low-timer TOP |
| `0x27` | `HPER` | `0xFF` | High-timer TOP |
| `0x28`, `0x2A`, `0x2C` | `LCMP0`, `LCMP1`, `LCMP2` | `0x00` | Low-timer compare values |
| `0x29`, `0x2B`, `0x2D` | `HCMP0`, `HCMP1`, `HCMP2` | `0x00` | High-timer compare values |

## 19. Checklist for later code generation

Before generating TCA code:

1. Select Normal or Split mode before interpreting the register map.
2. Stop TCA and issue RESET before changing between the two modes.
3. Determine actual `CLK_PER`, prescaler, required period, resolution, and permissible frequency error.
4. Select the correct `WGMODE` and its TOP, UPDATE, and `OVF` conditions.
5. Prefer `PERBUF` and `CMPnBUF` for live Normal-mode waveform changes.
6. Coordinate multi-channel changes with `LUPD`, `ALUPD`, or an explicit UPDATE command as required.
7. Resolve output pins and PORTMUX routes, then configure each associated PORT pin as an output before enabling its compare channel.
8. Establish safe output states before enabling TCA pin override.
9. Configure events only in Normal mode and verify the level-event frequency constraint.
10. Clear pending flags by direct write-one masks before enabling interrupts when required by the application.
11. Configure CPUINT and global interrupt state separately.
12. Decide Standby, Power-Down, and debug behavior.
13. Use verified AVR CPU 16-bit access rules for Normal-mode 16-bit registers.

## 20. Information not supplied by chapter 21

Chapter 21 does not by itself provide:

- package-specific waveform pins or PORTMUX route values;
- complete PORT initialization and safe board-level output states;
- clock-controller setup or actual `CLK_PER` accuracy;
- Event System channel and generator/user routing;
- CPUINT priority, ISR syntax, or global interrupt control;
- exact AVR CPU 16-bit register-access sequence and concurrency protection;
- compiler header names and constants;
- device errata or tested C examples.

These subjects require the corresponding local device materials, compiler headers, project hardware description, and later verified guidance.

# ATtiny1624/1626/1627 TCB - 16-bit Timer/Counter Type B

## 1. Purpose and source

This device-specific reference is derived from chapter 22, "TCB - 16-Bit Timer/Counter Type B," printed pages 243-265 of `../ATtiny1624-26-27-DataSheet-DS40002234B.pdf`, revision DS40002234B (2021). PDF and printed page numbers are the same for this range. The chapter was checked from extracted text and rendered pages.

This preliminary file summarizes only chapter 22. It does not select physical pins, configure PORT or PORTMUX, route Event System channels, define compiler-specific C symbols, provide tested drivers, or incorporate errata.

## 2. Peripheral structure

TCB is a 16-bit timer/counter with one 16-bit counter (`CNT`) and one 16-bit capture/compare register (`CCMP`). It supports periodic timing, timeout checking, four capture or measurement modes, single-shot waveform generation, and 8-bit PWM. Two TCB instances can be cascaded through the Event System for a 32-bit capture. [pp. 243-244]

The external TCB signal is the digital asynchronous waveform output `WO`. Its physical pin and alternate routes are defined outside chapter 22.

## 3. Terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `BOTTOM` | `CNT` becomes `0x0000` |
| `MAX` | `CNT` becomes `0xFFFF` |
| `TOP` | Highest value in the selected count sequence |
| `CNT` | `TCBn.CNT` counter value |
| `CCMP` | `TCBn.CCMP` capture/compare value |

## 4. Clocking and synchronization

`CTRLA.CLKSEL` selects the TCB clock: [pp. 244-245, 256]

| Value | Name | `CLK_TCB` source |
|---:|---|---|
| `0x0` | `DIV1` | `CLK_PER` |
| `0x1` | `DIV2` | `CLK_PER / 2` |
| `0x2` | `TCA0` | `CLK_TCA` from TCA0 |
| `0x3`-`0x6` | - | Reserved |
| `0x7` | `EVENT` | Positive edge on the `COUNT` event input |

Set `CTRLA.SYNCUPD` to restart TCB whenever its associated TCA restarts or overflows. If `CLKSEL = TCA0`, TCB follows that selected TCA clock and restart. With another clock selection, synchronization is with TCA0. This can align capture activity with a TCA PWM period. [pp. 252, 256]

TCB has two distinct Event System users: [pp. 252-253]

- `COUNT` supplies counter clock edges and is selected with `CLKSEL = EVENT`.
- `CAPT` triggers the mode-specific action and is enabled with `EVCTRL.CAPTEI`.

The general statement on page 245 that event-action operation requires the event channel as counter input must be read with this later distinction: a `CAPT` action does not by itself select the `COUNT` event as `CLK_TCB`.

## 5. Basic periodic initialization

TCB resets into Periodic Interrupt mode. The chapter gives this initialization sequence: [p. 245]

1. Write TOP to `TCBn.CCMP`.
2. Optionally set `TCBn.CTRLB.CCMPEN`; configure the corresponding PORT pin as an output first.
3. Select the required `CTRLA.CLKSEL` value.
4. Set `CTRLA.ENABLE`.
5. Read `TCBn.CNT` when required.

At `CNT = CCMP`, the `CAPT` flag and event are generated and the counter restarts from BOTTOM. If software lowers `CCMP` below the current `CNT`, equality with the new TOP has already been missed; the counter continues to MAX, sets `OVF`, wraps to BOTTOM, and then uses the new TOP.

Configure the required mode, events, output state, and flags before enabling the counter. The source recommends clearing `INTFLAGS` after configuration because configuration can set a flag. [p. 250]

## 6. Counter modes

`CTRLB.CNTMODE` selects one of eight modes. Do not change modes while TCB is enabled because the output can become unpredictable. [pp. 245-250, 257]

| Value | Name | Purpose | Role of `CCMP` |
|---:|---|---|---|
| `0x0` | `INT` | Periodic interrupt | 16-bit TOP |
| `0x1` | `TIMEOUT` | Timeout check between event edges | 16-bit TOP |
| `0x2` | `CAPT` | Capture counter on an event | Captured 16-bit count |
| `0x3` | `FRQ` | Measure period or frequency between selected edges | Captured 16-bit count |
| `0x4` | `PW` | Measure pulse width | Captured 16-bit count |
| `0x5` | `FRQPW` | Measure period and pulse width in one sequence | Captured width; `CNT` holds period |
| `0x6` | `SINGLE` | Generate one pulse per accepted event | 16-bit TOP |
| `0x7` | `PWM8` | 8-bit PWM | `CCMPL` period, `CCMPH` duty threshold |

### 6.1. Periodic Interrupt mode

The counter runs from BOTTOM to `CCMP` (TOP). Reaching TOP sets `CAPT` and restarts the counter at BOTTOM. `EDGE` and `CAPTEI` have no mode action. `OVF` is set only if the counter wraps from MAX because TOP was moved below the current count. [p. 246]

### 6.2. Timeout Check mode

The first selected event edge starts counting and the opposite edge stops and freezes the counter. With `EDGE = 0`, a positive edge starts and a negative edge stops; `EDGE = 1` reverses the polarities. If the counter reaches TOP before the stop edge, `CAPT` is set. In the frozen state, reading `CNT` or `CCMP`, or writing `STATUS.RUN`, has no effect on the counter state. [p. 246]

### 6.3. Input Capture on Event mode

The counter runs continuously from BOTTOM to MAX. A selected event edge copies `CNT` to `CCMP` and sets `CAPT`; counting continues. `EDGE = 0` selects a positive edge and `EDGE = 1` selects a negative edge. Reading `CCMPL`, the low byte of the capture value, clears `CAPT`. `OVF` is set on MAX-to-BOTTOM wrap. When entering this mode from any other mode, write `CNT = 0` as recommended by the source. [p. 247]

### 6.4. Frequency Measurement mode

A selected event edge copies `CNT` to `CCMP`, restarts the counter from BOTTOM, and sets `CAPT`. `EDGE` selects positive or negative edges. Reading `CCMPL` clears `CAPT`. `OVF` reports MAX-to-BOTTOM wrap. [p. 247]

### 6.5. Pulse-Width Measurement mode

With `EDGE = 0`, a positive edge clears and restarts the counter and the following negative edge captures the pulse width. With `EDGE = 1`, the polarities are reversed. Hardware switches the active edge automatically. Successive edges must be separated by at least two clock cycles. Reading `CCMPL` clears `CAPT`. [p. 248]

### 6.6. Frequency and Pulse-Width Measurement mode

With `EDGE = 0`: [p. 248]

1. First positive edge: clear and restart `CNT`.
2. Following negative edge: capture pulse width into `CCMP`.
3. Second positive edge: stop the counter with the period in `CNT` and set `CAPT`.

With `EDGE = 1`, all edge polarities are reversed. Read `CNT` first for the period and then read `CCMP` for the pulse width. Reading `CCMPL` clears `CAPT` and arms the next measurement; the counter resets at the next start edge.

### 6.7. Single-Shot mode

An accepted event starts a pulse and the counter. The output stays high while `CNT` counts from BOTTOM to `CCMP` (TOP), then the counter stops, the output becomes low, and `CAPT` is set. The output remains low for at least one `CLK_TCB` cycle; an event during this guard interval is ignored. [pp. 249-250]

- `EDGE = 0`: only a positive edge starts the pulse.
- `EDGE = 1`: either edge starts the pulse.
- `ASYNC = 0`: output goes high when the synchronized counter starts.
- `ASYNC = 1`: output goes high immediately when the event arrives; the counter still starts two to three `CLK_TCB` cycles later.

Enabling TCB, or modifying `EDGE` while enabled, starts the counter automatically in this mode. To prevent an unintended pulse, write TOP to `CNT` before enabling or changing `EDGE`.

### 6.8. 8-bit PWM mode

`CCMPL` and `CCMPH` operate as independent 8-bit values: [p. 250]

- `CCMPL` is TOP, so the PWM period is `CCMPL + 1` `CLK_TCB` cycles.
- `CCMPH` is the high-time threshold.
- The output is set at BOTTOM and cleared when `CNT = CCMPH`.
- `CAPT` is set on the duty compare condition.

Table 22-6 prints the identifiers `CCML` and `CCMH` for this mode, while the register description consistently defines `CCMPL` and `CCMPH`. This unresolved source naming problem is tracked as `PRB-TCB-001` in [Problems.md](../../../Problems.md).

## 7. Waveform output

Set `CTRLB.CCMPEN` to make the TCB waveform override the corresponding `PORTx.OUT` value. The PORT pin direction must be configured as output. [pp. 245, 250, 257]

| Mode | Output behavior when `CCMPEN = 1` |
|---|---|
| Single-Shot, `ASYNC = 0` | High when synchronized counting starts; low when counting stops |
| Single-Shot, `ASYNC = 1` | High immediately on event; low when counting stops |
| 8-bit PWM | PWM waveform |
| Other modes | Initial level selected by `CTRLB.CCMPINIT` |

`CCMPINIT` has no effect in Single-Shot or 8-bit PWM mode. With `CCMPEN = 0`, TCB does not drive the pin.

## 8. 32-bit input capture

Two TCBs can form a true 32-bit capture counter through the Event System. [pp. 250-252]

1. Configure the LSB TCB with the required count clock, an input-capture mode, and `CASCADE = 0`.
2. Route its `OVF` event to the MSB TCB `COUNT` user.
3. Configure the MSB TCB with `CLKSEL = EVENT`, the same capture mode, and `CASCADE = 1`.
4. Route the same capture event to both TCB `CAPT` users.
5. On capture, concatenate the registers as `(MSB_TCB.CCMP << 16) | LSB_TCB.CCMP`.

`CASCADE = 1` delays the MSB capture action by one `CLK_PER` cycle to compensate for carry propagation from the LSB overflow. See the derived [32-bit capture diagram](ATtiny162x_TCB_32_Bit_Capture.svg).

## 9. Input noise filter

Set `EVCTRL.FILTER` to accept a capture-event level only after four consecutive equal samples. The filter adds four `CLK_PER` cycles between an input change and capture-register update. It uses the peripheral clock and is not affected by the selected TCB prescaler. [p. 252]

## 10. Events

### 10.1. Event generators

TCB generates one-`CLK_PER`-period pulses when `CAPT` or `OVF` is set. Generator conditions are identical to the corresponding interrupt-flag conditions. [pp. 252-253]

### 10.2. Event users

| User | Enable or selection | Action |
|---|---|---|
| `CAPT` | `EVCTRL.CAPTEI = 1` | Mode-specific edge action selected by `EVCTRL.EDGE` and `CTRLB.CNTMODE` |
| `COUNT` | `CTRLA.CLKSEL = EVENT` | Positive event edge is the counter clock |

The synchronous capture path requires an event of at least one `CLK_PER` cycle. Asynchronous Single-Shot operation can detect a shorter edge-triggered event. [p. 253]

## 11. Interrupts and flags

`CAPT` and `OVF` share one TCB interrupt vector. `INTCTRL.CAPT` and `INTCTRL.OVF` enable the sources. `INTFLAGS.CAPT` and `INTFLAGS.OVF` are cleared by writing one. In capture modes, reading the capture value also clears `CAPT`; the mode descriptions specify the low-byte `CCMPL` read. [pp. 253, 259-260]

| Mode | `CAPT` set condition |
|---|---|
| Periodic Interrupt | Counter reaches TOP |
| Timeout Check | Counter reaches TOP |
| Input Capture on Event | Selected capture event loads `CCMP` |
| Frequency Measurement | Selected edge loads `CCMP` and restarts `CNT` |
| Pulse-Width Measurement | Capture edge loads `CCMP` |
| Frequency and Pulse-Width | Second same-polarity edge stops measurement |
| Single-Shot | Counter reaches TOP |
| 8-bit PWM | Counter reaches the duty compare value |

`OVF` is set whenever the 16-bit counter wraps from MAX to BOTTOM.

## 12. Sleep and debug behavior

- TCB halts in Standby by default.
- Set `CTRLA.RUNSTDBY` to keep TCB fully operational in Standby.
- All TCB operation halts in Power-Down.
- With `DBGCTRL.DBGRUN = 0`, TCB halts and ignores events in Break Debug mode.
- With `DBGCTRL.DBGRUN = 1`, TCB continues while the CPU is halted. [pp. 254, 262]

## 13. Register summary

| Offset | Register | Reset | Key contents |
|---:|---|---:|---|
| `0x00` | `CTRLA` | `0x00` | `RUNSTDBY`, `CASCADE`, `SYNCUPD`, `CLKSEL`, `ENABLE` |
| `0x01` | `CTRLB` | `0x00` | `ASYNC`, `CCMPINIT`, `CCMPEN`, `CNTMODE` |
| `0x04` | `EVCTRL` | `0x00` | `FILTER`, `EDGE`, `CAPTEI` |
| `0x05` | `INTCTRL` | `0x00` | `OVF`, `CAPT` interrupt enables |
| `0x06` | `INTFLAGS` | `0x00` | `OVF`, `CAPT`; write one to clear |
| `0x07` | `STATUS` | `0x00` | Read-only `RUN` state |
| `0x08` | `DBGCTRL` | `0x00` | `DBGRUN` |
| `0x09` | `TEMP` | `0x00` | Shared temporary byte for 16-bit accesses |
| `0x0A` | `CNT` | `0x0000` | 16-bit count (`CNTL`, `CNTH`) |
| `0x0C` | `CCMP` | `0x0000` | 16-bit capture/compare (`CCMPL`, `CCMPH`) |

`TEMP` is shared by all TCB 16-bit register accesses. CPU and UPDI writes to `CNT` have priority over internal updates. Exact read/write sequencing and atomicity rules are defined in the AVR CPU chapter, not chapter 22. [pp. 263-265]

## 14. Checklist for later code generation

Before generating TCB code:

1. Select the required TCB instance and verify it exists on the target device.
2. Select `CNTMODE` before assigning meaning to `CCMP`.
3. Determine the actual `CLK_PER`, TCB clock source, interval, resolution, and allowed error.
4. Distinguish the `CAPT` event action from the `COUNT` event clock.
5. Configure Event System routes separately when either event user is required.
6. Resolve the physical `WO` pin and PORTMUX route, set a safe PORT output state, and configure the pin as output before setting `CCMPEN`.
7. Do not change `CNTMODE` while TCB is enabled.
8. For capture modes, preserve the documented read order and `CAPT` auto-clear behavior.
9. For Single-Shot mode, account for synchronization latency, the one-cycle low guard interval, and the automatic start caused by enable or `EDGE` modification.
10. For 32-bit capture, configure both event paths and use `CASCADE` only on the MSB TCB.
11. Clear pending flags with direct write-one masks after configuration and before enabling interrupts when required.
12. Configure CPUINT and global interrupt state separately.
13. Decide Standby, Power-Down, and debug behavior.
14. Apply verified AVR CPU rules to 16-bit register accesses.
15. Check `PRB-TCB-001` before using the PWM8 names printed in Table 22-6.

title: ATtiny1624/1626/1627 TCB model
language: en

  file: ../ATtiny1624-26-27-DataSheet-DS40002234B.pdf
  document_revision: DS40002234B
  year: 2021
  chapter: 22
  chapter_title: TCB - 16-Bit Timer/Counter Type B
  printed_pages: "243-265"
  pdf_pages: "243-265"
  derivation: Summarized from extracted text and visually checked rendered pages.

applies_to: [ATtiny1624, ATtiny1626, ATtiny1627]

scope:
  included:
    - clock and synchronization controls
    - all eight counter modes
    - waveform output behavior
    - capture filtering and 32-bit cascading
    - events, interrupts, sleep, and debug behavior
    - register map and fields
  excluded:
    - package pins and PORTMUX values
    - complete PORT and clock-controller setup
    - Event System routing
    - CPUINT configuration
    - exact AVR CPU 16-bit access sequence
    - compiler symbols
    - errata
    - tested code

definitions:
  BOTTOM: Counter becomes 0x0000.
  MAX: Counter becomes 0xFFFF.
  TOP: Counter equals the highest value in the selected count sequence.
  CNT: TCBn.CNT register value.
  CCMP: TCBn.CCMP capture or compare value.

architecture:
  counter_width_bits: 16
  counter: TCBn.CNT
  capture_compare: TCBn.CCMP
  waveform_output: WO
  mode_count: 8
  thirty_two_bit_capture_supported: true

clock:
  selector: TCBn.CTRLA.CLKSEL
  choices:
    "0x0": {name: DIV1, source: CLK_PER}
    "0x1": {name: DIV2, source: CLK_PER / 2}
    "0x2": {name: TCA0, source: CLK_TCA from TCA0}
    "0x3-0x6": {name: RESERVED}
    "0x7": {name: EVENT, source: Positive edge on COUNT event input}
  enable: TCBn.CTRLA.ENABLE
  tca_synchronization:
    field: TCBn.CTRLA.SYNCUPD
    effect: Restart TCB whenever associated TCA restarts or overflows.
    tca_clock_selected: Restart with the selected TCA.
    other_clock_selected: Restart with TCA0.

event_user_distinction:
  CAPT:
    enable: TCBn.EVCTRL.CAPTEI
    purpose: Mode-specific edge action.
    controls: [TCBn.EVCTRL.EDGE, TCBn.CTRLB.CNTMODE]
  COUNT:
    selection: TCBn.CTRLA.CLKSEL=EVENT
    purpose: Positive event edges act as counter clock.
  interpretation_note: Selecting CAPT does not by itself select COUNT as CLK_TCB.

initialization_periodic:
  reset_mode: INT
  steps:
    - Write TOP to TCBn.CCMP.
    - Optionally configure the PORT pin as output and set TCBn.CTRLB.CCMPEN.
    - Select TCBn.CTRLA.CLKSEL.
    - Set TCBn.CTRLA.ENABLE.
  after_configuration: Clear required TCBn.INTFLAGS bits because configuration can set a flag.
  top_lowered_below_cnt:
    behavior: Counter continues to MAX, sets OVF, wraps to BOTTOM, then uses the new TOP.

modes:
  INT:
    value: "0x0"
    name: Periodic Interrupt
    ccmp_role: 16-bit TOP
    count_sequence: BOTTOM to CCMP, then BOTTOM
    capt_condition: CNT equals TOP
    edge_action: none
  TIMEOUT:
    value: "0x1"
    name: Time-out Check
    ccmp_role: 16-bit TOP
    capt_condition: CNT reaches TOP before stop edge
    edge_zero: {positive: start, negative: stop_and_freeze}
    edge_one: {positive: stop_and_freeze, negative: start}
    frozen_access_effect: Reading CNT or CCMP and writing STATUS.RUN do not change the state.
  CAPT:
    value: "0x2"
    name: Input Capture on Event
    ccmp_role: Captured 16-bit CNT
    count_sequence: BOTTOM to MAX continuously
    edge_zero: capture_on_positive
    edge_one: capture_on_negative
    capture_action: Copy CNT to CCMP and continue counting.
    entry_recommendation: Write CNT=0 when entering from any other mode.
    capt_auto_clear: Read CCMPL.
  FRQ:
    value: "0x3"
    name: Input Capture Frequency Measurement
    ccmp_role: Captured 16-bit CNT
    edge_zero: capture_on_positive
    edge_one: capture_on_negative
    capture_action: Copy CNT to CCMP and restart CNT from BOTTOM.
    capt_auto_clear: Read CCMPL.
  PW:
    value: "0x4"
    name: Input Capture Pulse-Width Measurement
    ccmp_role: Captured 16-bit pulse width
    edge_zero: {positive: clear_and_restart, negative: capture}
    edge_one: {negative: clear_and_restart, positive: capture}
    automatic_edge_switching: true
    minimum_edge_separation_clock_cycles: 2
    capt_auto_clear: Read CCMPL.
  FRQPW:
    value: "0x5"
    name: Input Capture Frequency and Pulse-Width Measurement
    ccmp_role: Captured 16-bit pulse width
    cnt_role_at_completion: Measured period
    edge_zero_sequence:
      - First positive edge clears and restarts CNT.
      - Following negative edge copies pulse width to CCMP.
      - Second positive edge stops CNT and sets CAPT.
    edge_one_sequence:
      - First negative edge clears and restarts CNT.
      - Following positive edge copies pulse width to CCMP.
      - Second negative edge stops CNT and sets CAPT.
    required_read_order: [CNT, CCMP]
    reason: Reading CCMPL clears CAPT and arms the next measurement.
  SINGLE:
    value: "0x6"
    name: Single-Shot
    ccmp_role: 16-bit TOP
    edge_zero: positive_starts
    edge_one: any_edge_starts
    output_sequence: High during count from BOTTOM to TOP, then low.
    capt_condition: CNT reaches TOP
    low_guard_minimum: One CLK_TCB cycle
    event_during_guard: ignored
    asynchronous_output:
      field: TCBn.CTRLB.ASYNC
      zero: Output becomes high when synchronized counting starts.
      one: Output becomes high immediately on event.
      counter_start_latency_when_one: Two to three CLK_TCB cycles.
    automatic_start_conditions:
      - Enable TCB.
      - Modify EDGE while TCB is enabled.
    prevent_unintended_start: Write TOP to CNT before enabling or changing EDGE.
  PWM8:
    value: "0x7"
    name: 8-bit PWM
    ccmp_role: CCMPL is period TOP and CCMPH is duty threshold.
    period_clock_cycles: CCMPL + 1
    output_at_bottom: set
    output_at_duty_compare: clear
    capt_condition: CNT equals duty compare value
    source_problem: PRB-TCB-001

output:
  enable: TCBn.CTRLB.CCMPEN
  enabled_effect: Override corresponding PORT output register.
  port_direction_requirement: Configure corresponding PORT pin as output.
  initial_value: TCBn.CTRLB.CCMPINIT
  initial_value_not_used_in: [SINGLE, PWM8]
  mode_change_while_enabled:
    recommended: false
    risk: Unpredictable output.

noise_filter:
  enable: TCBn.EVCTRL.FILTER
  acceptance_rule: Four consecutive equal event samples.
  additional_delay: Four CLK_PER cycles.
  clock: Peripheral clock
  affected_by_tcb_prescaler: false

cascade_32_bit_capture:
  lsb_tcb:
    count_source: Application-selected
    count_mode: Same input-capture mode as MSB TCB
    cascade: 0
    overflow_route: Route OVF event to MSB TCB COUNT user.
  msb_tcb:
    clock_select: EVENT
    count_mode: Same input-capture mode as LSB TCB
    cascade: 1
    cascade_effect: Delay CAPT action by one CLK_PER to compensate carry propagation.
  shared_capture_route: Route the same CAPT event to both TCBs.
  captured_value: "(MSB_TCB.CCMP << 16) | LSB_TCB.CCMP"

events:
  generators:
    CAPT:
      condition: Same as CAPT interrupt flag.
      type: pulse
      clock_domain: CLK_PER
      duration: One CLK_PER period
    OVF:
      condition: Same as OVF interrupt flag.
      type: pulse
      clock_domain: CLK_PER
      duration: One CLK_PER period
  users:
    CAPT:
      detection: edge
      synchronous_modes: [TIMEOUT, CAPT, FRQ, PW, FRQPW]
      both_sync_and_async_modes: [SINGLE]
      synchronous_minimum_event_length: One CLK_PER cycle
      async_single_shot_accepts_shorter_event: true
    COUNT:
      detection: positive_edge
      synchronization: sync

interrupts:
  vector: One shared TCB vector
  sources:
    CAPT:
      enable: TCBn.INTCTRL.CAPT
      flag: TCBn.INTFLAGS.CAPT
      clear: Write one, or read capture value in a capture mode.
    OVF:
      enable: TCBn.INTCTRL.OVF
      flag: TCBn.INTFLAGS.OVF
      condition: Counter wraps from MAX to BOTTOM.
      clear: Write one.

sleep:
  standby_default: halted
  standby_with_runstdby: fully_operational
  power_down: halted

debug:
  register: TCBn.DBGCTRL.DBGRUN
  values:
    0: Peripheral halts in Break Debug mode and ignores events.
    1: Peripheral continues while CPU is halted.

registers:
  CTRLA:
    offset: "0x00"
    reset: "0x00"
    fields: {RUNSTDBY: 6, CASCADE: 5, SYNCUPD: 4, CLKSEL: "3:1", ENABLE: 0}
  CTRLB:
    offset: "0x01"
    reset: "0x00"
    fields: {ASYNC: 6, CCMPINIT: 5, CCMPEN: 4, CNTMODE: "2:0"}
  EVCTRL:
    offset: "0x04"
    reset: "0x00"
    fields: {FILTER: 6, EDGE: 4, CAPTEI: 0}
  INTCTRL:
    offset: "0x05"
    reset: "0x00"
    fields: {OVF: 1, CAPT: 0}
  INTFLAGS:
    offset: "0x06"
    reset: "0x00"
    clear: write_one
    fields: {OVF: 1, CAPT: 0}
  STATUS:
    offset: "0x07"
    reset: "0x00"
    fields: {RUN: {bit: 0, access: read_only}}
  DBGCTRL:
    offset: "0x08"
    reset: "0x00"
    fields: {DBGRUN: 0}
  TEMP:
    offset: "0x09"
    reset: "0x00"
    width_bits: 8
    description: Shared temporary byte for CPU access to all TCB 16-bit registers.
  CNT:
    offset: "0x0A"
    reset: "0x0000"
    width_bits: 16
    byte_names: [CNTL, CNTH]
    write_priority_over_internal_update: true
  CCMP:
    offset: "0x0C"
    reset: "0x0000"
    width_bits: 16
    byte_names: [CCMPL, CCMPH]

source_discrepancies:
  - id: PRB-TCB-001
    status: unresolved
    location: Table 22-6, printed/PDF page 260
    printed_names: [CCML, CCMH]
    register_description_names: [CCMPL, CCMPH]
    safe_interpretation: Treat the table row as unresolved source terminology; use the documented register byte names CCMPL and CCMPH in derived explanations.

code_generation_checklist:
  - Select an available TCB instance and required CNTMODE.
  - Calculate settings from actual CLK_PER and selected clock source.
  - Distinguish the CAPT event action from the COUNT event clock.
  - Configure Event System routes separately.
  - Resolve WO pin and PORTMUX, then establish a safe PORT output before CCMPEN.
  - Do not change CNTMODE while enabled.
  - Preserve capture read order and flag-clear behavior.
  - Account for Single-Shot latency and guard interval.
  - Configure CASCADE only on the MSB TCB in a 32-bit pair.
  - Clear pending flags by writing one after configuration.
  - Configure CPUINT and global interrupt state separately.
  - Apply verified AVR CPU 16-bit register-access rules.
  - Check PRB-TCB-001 before using Table 22-6 PWM8 identifiers.

# ATtiny1624/1626/1627 TCB Source Guide

This file is the starting point for work with the 16-bit Timer/Counter Type B (TCB) on ATtiny1624, ATtiny1626, and ATtiny1627.

## Current reading order

1. Read [ATtiny162x_TCB_16_Bit_Timer_Counter_Type_B.md](ATtiny162x_TCB_16_Bit_Timer_Counter_Type_B.md) for device-specific behavior derived from data sheet chapter 22.
2. Use [ATtiny162x_TCB_Model.yaml](ATtiny162x_TCB_Model.yaml) for structured mode, clock, event, interrupt, and register data.
3. Use the [block diagram](ATtiny162x_TCB_Block_Diagram.svg), [mode overview](ATtiny162x_TCB_Mode_Overview.svg), [capture timing diagram](ATtiny162x_TCB_Capture_Timing.svg), and [32-bit capture diagram](ATtiny162x_TCB_32_Bit_Capture.svg) for signal and timing relationships.
4. Check [Problems.md](../../../Problems.md) before relying on a source detail marked as unresolved.
5. If a required hardware fact is absent or unclear, inspect only the relevant pages of the [ATtiny1624/1626/1627 data sheet](../ATtiny1624-26-27-DataSheet-DS40002234B.pdf), starting with chapter 22, printed pages 243-265.

This preliminary guide uses only the local data sheet chapter and the derived files listed above. Pin routing, complete PORT and PORTMUX configuration, Event System routing, CPU interrupt policy, compiler symbols, tested code patterns, CPU 16-bit access details, errata, and external application guidance must be obtained from their corresponding local materials or added later.

title: ATtiny1624/1626/1627 USART model
language: en

source:
  file: ../ATtiny1624-26-27-DataSheet-DS40002234B.pdf
